speakeroldname: Mr. H. O. While (Middlesex East) moved
speechtext:
that the first report of the standing committee on external affairs, presented to the house on Tuesday, February 23, 1960, be now concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is one of the routine motions, and in the past I have given my word to the committee that we would try at all times to hold the meetings of the committee at times when the house was not sitting. In the two previous sessions we were able to do this with the exception of one occasion, and that occasion was when General McNaughton of the international joint commission was presenting his report to the committee, which necessitated a meeting so that General McNaughton could go to Washington on the business of the commission.
During the years when the opposition were the government of the day I cannot recall any occasion, and I know they will correct me if I am wrong, when they did not ask for leave to sit while the house was sitting. Yesterday the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) asked the committee not to sit while

External Affairs Committee the house was sitting. He put forward that plea, and then later that same day said he would be going to call General Burns as a witness, because he was going abroad and it was necessary to have General Burns appear before us.
Of course the first argument does not hold water; but with regard to the other, I know General Burns has many important duties to perform, and it might be just possible that he would be unable to attend on two or three days and consequently it would be necessary to have the committee sit while the house was sitting.
Therefore I move this motion, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. gentleman who is the chairman of this committee. I would simply say in reply that if the situation which he spoke of regarding General Burns should arise, as we on the committee hope it will, and it is necessary to sit for a protracted period, it can always be so arranged and I am sure will be agreed to unanimously. But we have to consider, as the Prime Minister said last year when speaking in this house, I think on February 13, that the first duty of all of us lies in this chamber, and that nothing should develop which would preclude any hon. member from properly discharging his duties in this House of Commons. That being the case, I regret that we cannot support the motion which the hon. gentleman has moved.
When this matter came to the attention of the house at the previous session of parliament the same effort was made early in the session that is being made at the present time. This session has just begun its work, and much lies before us in this chamber. Hon. gentlemen in the opposition, and certainly in the Liberal party, find it very difficult to discharge our functions if we are obliged to face a situation in which committees are meeting while the house is sitting.
It will not be forgotten that at one time in 1958 no fewer than six committees were sitting simultaneously while the house itself was in session, making it impossible for members to attend properly either in committee or in the house.
What did you do?

The hon. member asks what we did. I think the situation then was altogether different from the situation now, but whether it was different or not the fact remains that we ought to be able to address ourselves to the merits of each question as it is presented, regardless of what was done on other occasions in the past.
We had exactly the same number of members as you have in the house now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. This motion is debatable and the hon. member who has the floor is entitled to be heard.

When hon. gentlemen opposite bring us, as they always do, the argument of precedent, one can only find in that a recognition that whatever the previous administration did was, apparently, always right.
I address my remarks to the Prime Minister, who along with yourself, Mr. Speaker, is the chief custodian of the rights and privileges of parliament. The Prime Minister, I am sure, who is anxious to see to it that members opposite, as well as members on this side, are given the fullest opportunity to discharge their responsibilities properly, will, I am sure, recognize the validity of the plea which I so amiably present to him. I will remind the right hon. gentleman of his own words as recorded at page 990 of Hansard of last year:
I for one will say unequivocally that if at any time there is any action taken which would deny members of the opposition a fair opportunity of discharging their responsibilities I shall immediately see to it that a change is made to assure justice and fairness.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that this is a case to which he might apply those wise observations made on another occasion; and while I understand it is difficult for him to take issue with the members of his party, this is one occasion when in the interests of this house he should unhesitatingly line up with the opposition.

Members of this group wholeheartedly support the protest of the hon. member for Essex East. On several occasions recently we have found ourselves making hay together on behalf of democratic principles. However, I want to say this; that while hon. members who support the government and hon. members of the official opposition accuse each other of delinquencies in this connection in the past, our record is without blemish.
I listened with interest to what the chairman of the committee had to say in support of his motion. We respect the hon. member very much indeed. He is one of the "whitest" chairmen I have ever known. But we do take strong exception to this procedure. We support the reasons for this attitude given by the hon. member for Essex East. We think it is wrong in principle to ask, so early in the session, that committees should sit while the house itself is sitting.

There is a heavy and important agenda this session. As the hon. member for Essex East has said, the first responsibility of hon. members is in this house to attend these debates and, where an hon. member considers it necessary, to participate in them. We think this motion should be moved only when necessary to suit the convenience of witnesses coming from distant places, or the convenience of representatives of various organizations from across the country. There are occasions when it is necessary. Also, possibly it is necessary at the conclusion of the session when it is required to finish the business with as much dispatch as possible.
For the reasons mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East, and for the additional reasons I have advanced, we take the strongest exception to the adoption of this motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. Nesbiti (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. members for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I would point out that on this occasion we are dealing with a motion relating to the sittings of the committee on external affairs rather than to sittings of committees generally.
I should like to point out, as the hon. member for Middlesex East, who is chairman of this committee, has already done, that as a result of the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Essex East the committee might like to call General Burns, for instance, as a witness. If the committee should decide so to do this would have to be done in the very early stages. I believe all hon. members know that the 10-power disarmament committee commences its meetings on March 15, and the committee on external affairs cannot likely begin its sittings before early in March. Consequently if General Burns were to be called as a witness he would have to be called at an early date, and undoubtedly if he were called it would be necessary for the committee to hear him when the house was in session.
I cannot understand how the arguments of the hon. member for Essex East, which may possibly apply to committees generally, could apply in this particular case. In view of his own suggestion it would seem manifestly strange to me if we should not adopt this motion at the present time. If the house does not adopt this motion at this time, then possibly at the very first or second meeting of this committee permission would have to be requested from the house to enable the committee to sit while the house is in session 79951-0-91
External Affairs Committee in order to hear a witness who the hon. member serving as opposition spokesman indicates he wishes to have called before the committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I may say a word on this. The hon. member for Essex East has urged that we approach this question with reason. I suggest that we follow that course. The hon. gentleman does not like to go by precedent. In order that the house may be informed and the record kept straight, and without saying whether it was right or wrong, let me outline the situation that obtained in 1956. In that year, when the hon. member for Essex East and those in his party were enjoying their second last year of office, there were 152 days devoted to the business of that session. On 52 of those days the committees of the house met during the period when the house was in session.
At the end of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This occurred during the session, because the power to sit while the house was in session was granted to committees of the house quite early in the session. If you compare the record for 1956 with that for 1959 you will find a marked similarity. In 1959 there were 127 sitting days in the session. On 55 of those days committees of the house met while the house was in session. We followed what has been the practice of this house for many years.
It is impossible to carry on the committee meetings without sometimes coming into conflict with the sittings of the house. Mark you, it is preferable if it can be arranged otherwise, but that is not always possible. I recall that in 1955 or 1956 one of those periodical articles appeared in the press pointing out that there were not many hon. members sitting in the chamber, and on that very day there were 100 members of the house engaged in committee work; but that, of course, escaped notice.
That pattern occurs from time to time, and I do not know any way in which it can be avoided. There are so many problems that have to be taken up in committee. I believe it should be left to the good sense of the committee as to whether it can meet without interfering with the business of the house. But there are certain limitations. One is the number of rooms that are available for committee work. If the building were enlarged and there were more committee space available, perhaps there would not be these conflicts.
I think it would be wrong not to give the power immediately and leave it to the good
1434	HOUSE OF
Banking and Commerce Committee sense of the committee whether or not that power is used. Otherwise, if power is not given to sit while the house is in session and the committee has to come back to get that permission from the house, there will inevitably be delays. Apparently my hon. friends are going to raise this issue as to some of the other committees, but everyone knows that there are people called to appear before committees whose time should not be consumed in simply waiting for a committee to meet. There are several examples; the head of the C.N.R., the head of T.C.A., members of the wheat board, members of the board of grain commissioners. I have been a member of committees myself, so I know exactly what happens. When a committee meets two or three times during the course of a day the result is that within two days these busy businessmen are released to carry on their normal duties.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I submit it is only proper that this committee and other committees should be given this power in exactly the same way.

Mr. Speaker, without doubt this is a most important matter. There can be no question about that whatever. Recognizing that, could I through you, sir, make an appeal to all members to keep all speeches and technicalities down to a minimum, as this is the last day under the special order for Bill No. C-6 to come before the house. I would hate to see something that can be discussed at other times be responsible for preventing full discussion of that bill.

I also drew to the attention of the Prime Minister what had happened in the 1958 session when this committee was dealing with the estate tax legislation. That legislation was the responsibility of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and notwithstanding an appeal made to him and to the chairman of the committee the minister persisted in having the committee sit while the house was sitting. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) had very important business before the house at that time, with the result that it was not possible for certain members to attend properly to both the business before the banking and commerce committee and the trade and commerce matters that were then before the house.
So far as I am aware there is no reason for leave to be given to this committee to sit while the house is in session. speechtext:
I should like to ask a question preceding the discussion later this day on Bill No. C-6. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would consider recommending to the house a further day for debate on this bill, which deals with capital punishment, if at the end of today's debate

Inquiries of the Ministry there are members who have not had an opportunity to take part in that debate. My purpose in asking the Prime Minister this question is to ensure that no decision will be taken on this matter until those members who wish to state their position in regard to it have had an opportunity of so doing.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL DAY FOR DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: It is a coincidence, but I have written out very much the same type of question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL DAY FOR DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps before the coincidence becomes apparent I might answer the question, and then no doubt the hon. gentleman will express his views on the matter.
In my 20 years' experience in the house I do not know that I have seen the same degree of interest in any matter coming before the house that has been shown in this debate. The Leader of the Opposition asks me whether, under all the circumstances, another day later on might be provided. I am sure there are many who wish to take part in the debate, because the question of capital punishment is one that transcends ordinary considerations and touches the conscience of individual members. This means that many members, who under ordinary circumstances would allow others to express their views in a matter of the nature of capital punishment would not be willing to give up their right to place their individual views before the house and the country.
I have asked for the list of prospective participants in the debate. This list of prospective participants in the debate covers only, of course, the members on the government side of the house, and they are some 40 in number. There are members in other parts of the house who are equally desirous of expressing themselves. The hour is now 3.15 p.m. No member would like to be placed in the position, however strong his personal predilections on the subject may be, of in any way, however conscientious his desire to speak, having done anything that would prevent a vote taking place on this subject.
This being so, and in order to guard against the possibility of members being placed in the invidious position to which I have just alluded, if the house were agreeable I would suggest that all members desiring to participate should be able to do so. If at 10 o'clock this evening there are still members desirous of speaking, then I would feel it would be proper that another day be set aside later on so the fullest and most comprehensive consideration of this matter would be given by parliament. In other words there should be no curtailment of the right of hon. members to debate. Of course, this being a private member's bill there is nothing I can

do to determine that course. In view of the question of the Leader of the Opposition I would certainly agree that his suggestion is a meritorious one.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL DAY FOR DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I might say that the statement made by the Prime Minister is most agreeable to the members of this party. I think I would be at liberty to say that I have already expressed privately to the house leader views along this line, namely that if it were impossible to conclude the debate today and have a vote, members who are desirous of speaking should have an opportunity to speak. I was certain this could be brought about by agreement amongst the three parties to set aside a further day.
This, as the Prime Minister has said, is an important public question that touches the conscience of the members of this house, and in which there is very great public interest. I believe the first day of debate on this question showed parliament at its best. Members spoke from great conviction, and there was no endeavour to follow party lines. This being the case, I think the Prime Minister's suggestion is most agreeable. We are quite happy to make provision for another day of debate, and we think this further obliges the House of Commons that at some stage of the debate on this bill the question shall be put.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. McGee for the second reading of Bill No. C-6 to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like probably 80 per cent of the people of Canada I was conspicuously uninterested in the abolition of capital punishment until I was confronted with the necessity of making a decision. After searching my conscience and all the literature I could find on the subject I believe I should vote against this motion.
I believe that abolition is advocated by a small, sincere, but vociferous minority such as promoted prohibition, when the great mass of the people who favoured temperance, not abstinence, were not heard. I know that all advances are made by a creative minority and that I shall probably be branded as a philistine, but I am not one of those who confuse all -change with progress.
I believe this question is typical of certain degenerate and dangerous ideas current in this century and especially on this continent. Like the Deweyite theories in education which are turning out a generation of educated illiterates, we are uncritically swallowing whole the half-baked ideas of the psychologists and sociologists that anyone who commits a murder must be sick; that the action of such people is due entirely to their heredity and environment and that, therefore, they are not responsible.
There is a certain truth in the notion of corporate guilt, and society must share part

Capital Punishment
of the blame for any antisocial actions. We are all the victims of our heredity and our environment while we dwell in time and space. Many inherit recessive genes resulting in a weak mind or a weak will. Many suffer a squalid environment; and I may say the underprivileged or overindulged rich are in some respects worse off than those who were brought up in pride and poverty.
Despite these factors there must remain some residue of free will or there is no responsibility. If we have no responsibility, we are not men but automatons. There is only one sense in which this grim predestination is true, and that is the Calvinist and, indeed, Catholic belief that an omnipotent God must know our ultimate destiny before we are even conceived. This dull determinism which negates all responsibility reduces our humanity and cannot be accepted by any civilization which is to survive.
To me the only valid argument the abolitionists have is the possibility of mistake. All things human are fallible, and innocent men have been hanged. But I believe that is very rare. Lord Justice Darling of the English bench and privy council said to the House of Commons committee in 1930 that 26 years' experience on the bench had convinced him that in view of the checks and safeguards of English law it is practically impossible for an innocent man to be hanged, although a great many guilty ones escape; but that the knowledge that a person is liable to be hanged for committing a murder undoubtedly has a deterrent effect.
I have always been concerned that the verdict of any court seems to depend more on the relative eloquence of contending counsel than on the merits of the case. Some amendments to criminal law or procedure, such as introducing degrees of homicide, with the death penalty retained only for first degree murder, may be desirable. I do not believe, however, that there should be a discretion left to the judge or jury to specify death or imprisonment. One week a jury would let the murderer off; the next jury would hang him. Even judges would be inconsistent. Criminal justice must be conducted according to fixed and known standards, not by popular clamour or individual caprice.
The present system of administration of justice involves trial by judge and jury. If the verdict is "guilty" the prisoner may appeal to the court of appeal on any ground of law for a new trial, and to the Supreme Court of Canada if the court of appeal is not unanimous. If the verdict is upheld the prisoner's counsel may, and generally does, appeal to the governor general in council for executive clemency on any ground whatever. The

Minister of Justice thereupon obtains the full record of the case, always with a report from the trial judge, especially concerning any mitigating circumstances such as the jury's recommendation of mercy and any other reports necessary. The whole matter is then considered by the departmental expert in criminal affairs, then by the deputy minister of justice, then by the minister himself, and his report is considered by the whole cabinet. The minister then advises the Governor General to confirm or commute the sentence. The prisoner has then three months in which to prepare for death, a period longer than that in which the repentant thief on the cross found pardon and peace.
Although the present system of administration is probably quite adequate, I believe the whole substantive law on insanity requires a thorough overhaul in the light of modem medical and psychological insights. The law contends that irresistible impulse is unresisted impulse and that a person is insane and, therefore, innocent if he would attempt murder with a policeman at his elbow. This is plausible, but it does not go deep enough. The Macnaughton rules for determining guilt need revising.
Modern criminology recognizes four aims of punishments; protective, deterrent, reformative and retributive. Obviously if a murderer is hanged, society is completely protected from his repeating his crime on his escape or reprieve. I refer to the cases of Red Ryan and Courtauld. If the number of long term prisoners were substantially increased the chances of their again committing murder would be increased in their attempting to escape prison or recapture or by making a livelihood from armed robbery. It is important at this stage to remember that we would be dealing with desperate men who had nothing further to lose.
The deterrent effect of the death penalty on others is inconclusive, I admit, although I do believe it is significant that the home secretary of Great Britain, Mr. R. A. Butler, admitted that indictable crimes had risen by 14.8 per cent and robberies by 29 per cent since Great Britain modified its capital punishment law in 1957. At least it can be said that the psychic shock of hanging is as great a deterrent as that of life imprisonment.
What about reformation? The whole rationale of abolishing the death penalty is based on the sanctity of human life, yet there is a shocking discrepancy between a cold blooded murder and a few years' imprisonment. To have the support of society, justice must not only be done but must appear to be done, and there must be a right proportion between the penalty imposed and the gravity of the offence.

If one is to have due regard to the sanctity of human life and not outrage the sensitivity of society, the only alternative to the death sentence is life imprisonment, literally, without any reprieve. If the murderer repents and reforms he has greater scope to make restitution in prison by helping others reform than he would have outside. But is not a quick and dramatic exit from this life, after due time to prepare for death, less cruel than condemning one to be a living ghost, and condemning others to the half-life of a prison guard?
Retribution has now been discredited, but I am not so sure that there is not something to be said in favour of certain aspects of it. People say that we are now too civilized for vengeance, yet in this age we caused thousands of women and children to die a terrible death at Hiroshima and our enemies murdered 6 million innocent Jews with cool, clinical detachment in a most hygienic, scientific way.
The words of Christ, "Let him who is without sin cast the first stone", will be quoted many times in this debate. But Christ also said, "With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you", and the scriptures which Christ came to fulfil state, "For blood, it defileth the earth, and the earth cannot be cleansed but by the blood of him that shed it".
I think it is significant that only one church in Canada, to my knowledge, has come out unequivocally, as a church, in expressing itself in favour of the complete abolition of the death penalty. It is also significant that this church does not emphasize that lofty tragic view of life of the older churches whose theology is in such accord with the essential nature and destiny of man.
Sir Walter Moberly, although he is against the death penalty for murder, states the case for retribution very clearly in these words:
It is the function of the state to "stigmatize crime, not only as dangerous to the perpetrator, but as execrably wicked. It seeks not only to demonstrate that crime is 'an ill-bargain for the offender', but to excite against it a sentiment of horror."-"It is the verdict rather than the sentence which matters most". But the verdict is embodied in dramatic action. "The execution of the murderer is a solemn ritual act. Its object is not only to demonstrate that murder does not pay but to stamp it as shameful. The penalty is not only death but death with ignominy." And finally "the moral status of capital punishment will depend not on what it is in itself, but on what it signifies. The real test is not its direct effect in deterring potential murderers but its long term influence on the conscience of the community."
Let me attempt to express it in my own words in this manner. When a brutal murder is committed and no one is apprehended the feelings of a sensitive, civilized community
Ca-pital Punishment
are, and should be, profoundly shocked. The whole basis of order for which society was originally founded is frustrated and the law is brought into disrepute. This, I contend is a completely legitimate reaction. Similarly if through the incompentence of a crown prosecutor or the perverseness of a jury the accused against whom all the evidence points in a murder gets off scot-free, the community is outraged. This is also a legitimate reaction. If a person convicted of a brutal murder is given a life sentence which will be commuted in 10 or 15 years and the community is equally shocked, is not their reaction justified? Call it retribution, vengeance, or what you will.
If a convicted murderer is not executed but is imprisoned for life, the result is that the criminal is housed, fed, clothed, educated and amused for life at the expense of the state, whereas the wife and family of the murdered policeman or other quiet citizen have nothing done for them. Is this just or right?
Some will say that money and human life cannot be equated. Very well, then, Mr. Speaker; let the convicted murderer be executed and the money that would have been spent on his life imprisonment given to the next of kin of his murdered victim, since society is implicated in every crime and we are our brother's keepers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss indeed if I did not with my very first words congratulate the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) upon bringing this very important bill before the house. A week ago today when he made his presentation I thought that he should be congratulated not only on the

Capital Punishment
ground he covered but for the excellent way he dealt with the bill he was presenting. I would also be remiss if I did not congratulate all hon. members who have taken part in the debate so far. I think it is one of the finest and most intelligent debates I have listened to, with no political bitterness whatsoever entering into it.
I was particularly impressed by the speech made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney). Of course, he is acknowledged to be not only a successful but, indeed, a brilliant lawyer in the city of Toronto and the province of Ontario. I thought the way he covered the subject was not only intelligent but very informative to all members of the house. I would not want to say that the other speeches were not equally as good as 1 think everybody who has taken part in the debate has done a lot of research on the subject and they deserve much credit.
In taking part in the debate I must start out in a way I do not like to, in an apologetic tone, and say to members of the house that I do not regard myself as an authority on capital punishment in general or hanging in particular. We all know that there is certainly nothing pleasant about discussing crime generally or murder in particular, but we do have crime because of failures. To me those failures include failure to prevent delinquency, failure to correct delinquency, and certainly beyond that there is failure to detect crime and to prosecute the criminal.
Ordinarily when one comes to discuss a legal matter, as this question of capital punishment certainly is, one does so coldly, logically, without heat and, indeed, from the head and from the heart. Of course, there are logical approaches which one may consider if one cares to, those cold things called statistics which can be made to prove anything. As I have read some of the statistics I have come to the conclusion that the incidence of violent crime seems not to be greatly affected whether or not the threat of the gallows is present.
There is also in my estimation purely as a layman what I think could be described as the economic approach under which it is generally conceded that at least some murderers are worthless individuals from whom society should be protected, and it may be a fair question as to how much society should pay for the protection to which it is admittedly entitled. Should it pay the slight and final cost of the hangman and the rope or the very great cost of keeping the proved deliberate killer in confinement for his natural life or until authority is otherwise pleased? This of course raises the question whether it is safe to let loose again on society one who,

at least in circumstances which may recur, will be moved to kill again. If he is to be kept forever in custody, is that for the benefit of anyone, even himself, and if he is ever to be released, who shall weigh the risk?
Then there is the religious approach, if it may be so described, to which so many hon. members have referred. Certainly it is at least the biblical one. "Who sheddeth man's blood, by man let his blood be shed." So I come back to where I started, to my emotions rather than to my cold feelings with regard to the bill, and I am sure that other members have encountered this difficulty.
I was greatly interested in reading the book, "The Shadow of the Gallows", by Viscount Templewood, who was home secretary from 1937 to 1939. On capital punishment he has this to say:
Mr. Quintin Hogg, like everyone else, hated the death penalty. But the house would be clothed with "dishonour and humiliation" if it abolished it now, having acquiesced in the Nuremberg executions. The irrevocability of the penalty was a reason for every possible precaution against injustice, not for abolition. As regards deterrence, "statistics are not cogent... Patiently, honourably and scrupulously collected as they have been they only fuddle us." He preferred to look into his own heart, and there he found that if he were a professional burglar, with terms of penal servitude behind him and no death penalty to fear, he would take the chance of carrying a gun and shooting any witness of his crime.
We only have to refer back to some of the crimes of the past such as the case of Crippen and certainly that of Mrs. Thompson-I am sure the hon. member for Parkdale is well aware of these cases-to consider that theirs were crimes of sudden passion or of torment. Then there was the case of Sedden who poisoned an old and trusting woman for a few pitiful pounds, and the case of Laroque who insured the young farm labourer Bergeron for a few thousand dollars and then brutally murdered him. I have no faith that even the longest term in prison would reform such a person and I would think the result of failure too great to permit an experiment. If they are not to be reformed, if they are to die slowly in prison rather than quickly and humanely on the gallows, is that life or is it rather a living death?
Society has its rights and as individuals we have our rights, and it seems to me that it is the right and, indeed, may well be the duty of society to purge itself of those elements which are dangerous to it and my heart and my deepest instincts tell me that for some murderers death is the proper punishment.
Just a few days ago-I think it was last Monday-I was very much interested in reading a report in the Buffalo Courier respecting a bill now before the California senate and legislature to abolish capital punishment. In

polling the California senators and legislators with respect to this bill the result was that 21 of the 41 senators in that state said that they would vote against legislation to ban capital punishment. Nine said that they would vote for such a bill and seven took no stand. In the legislature 78 members were polled. Thirty three were against capital punishment, 16 for and five took no stand whatsoever. I might add that in the California legislature bills to ban the death penalty have been defeated eight times in the last 27 years. Many of the lawmakers of that state claimed that the issue of the death penalty should be decided by the people and suggested that it should be placed on the ballot in the coming November election in the United States.
My approach to the bill before us or to the question under discussion has been that of a conscientious citizen of this country. I am deeply intent, as I am sure other members of the house are, upon raising the national standard of dignity and morals, and one who studies the facts of both the past and the present should base his conclusions on actual experience rather than theory and sentiment. I cannot help but feel from reading statements in the papers and listening to the splendid speeches in the house pertaining to the bill that the opinion of the majority of judges, prison governors and police officers is against the abolition of the death penalty. Certainly their views are entitled to the fullest measure of respect. These gentlemen see the worst side of human nature and their primary duty is the maintenance of law and order. The result is that almost invariably they have been nervous about changes in our penal methods, though evidence has shown at times that at least some of their fears were groundless.
Many people are either for or against the bill, and I certainly do not want to say that they have reached their opinion through ignorance but rather on their reluctance to study the facts. For many years penal questions, and particularly the question of capital punishment, have often been treated with indifference or have been submerged in a highly charged atmosphere of sentiment and prejudice.
It must be a terrific strain and burden, not only on a judge or jury but on the cabinet itself, when they have to consider the question of whether a murderer is to die or will be given life imprisonment. What I hope is that this government will give us some leadership and that they will bring in a definite bill amending the Criminal Code which would speak with authority, clearness and compulsion. Some of the people who consider capital punishment necessary consider the method of execution in Canada and elsewhere
Capital Punishment
as inhuman, indeed, as a barbarous method. Many people have asked that some other method be devised such as the electric chair or gas chamber, because they consider such methods less gruesome than hanging. However, whatever method is used, if it is to be a punishment or a deterrent, it should be as effective as possible.
Any suggestion of an alternative to the death penalty should include an initial reference to a preventative which would give considerable attention to the identification of potential murderers, and other serious offenders, upon their first contact with the law, with a view to treatment or long term incarceration designed to prevent the commission of more serious acts. Dr. Joseph Cotton, who was considered an authority on this subject and who made a detailed study of many of the case histories of prisoners, believes that 40 per cent of murderers in the United States could have been detected and their crimes prevented by proper treatment when the offender first came into contact with the law.
Those who oppose the substitution of life imprisonment for the death penalty have given many reasons for their opposition. They mention the difficulty of preventing escape; the effect which the convicted murderer is apt to have upon other inmates and the cost of keeping that murderer. They suggest that life imprisonment is less humane than killing and refer to the danger associated with the inmate's eventual release in the community. Those who oppose capital punishment answer that these offenders may be kept in special security cells and taught a trade while they are being treated. I read an article not very long ago which had been written by the late Warden E. Lawes of Sing Sing prison. He stated that murderers make the best prisoners. They are the least troublesome to any warden and often accomplish a great deal behind bars. I also noted that he stated, and I quote:
I know of no convicted murderers released during my period in Sing Sing who reverted to crime.
As I said during the throne speech debate, in my opinion, this bill is one of the most important that has come before the house in many years. I was quite amused a day or two later to see an editorial to the effect that it was thought I had exaggerated the case to some extent. I was very happy, therefore, to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) say that this was one of the most important bills to come before the house in the last 20 years, and to hear the leader of the C.C.F. agree with him. Certainly when one man deliberately murders another the question arises, not only with the government but with parliament itself, what is to be done

Capital Punishment
about it? The paramount question is, how should the murderer be treated in the interest of peace, order, public safety and, last but not least, good government. This problem faces me as an ordinary layman, and is one that cannot easily be solved simply by argument, reason or facts. It is a case simply of one hon. member's opinion against another. However, these opinions must be based on facts, consideration, good judgment and good understanding. In addition, we cannot escape from the fact that sentiment, conscience and feeling are involved.
Many people claim, and I do not agree with this, that the reason we do have murderers is that too often the Canadian home does not occupy its proper place in our national life as it did at the turn of the century. They say we are in a state of moral depression and that the breakdown of the home is both a cause and a result. In many instances, any resemblance of religious training is barred in these homes and the mention of God is frowned upon, while espousers of godless communism carry on under the guise of academic freedom. I want to be clear and state definitely that I have read many articles on this subject. The ones that have impressed me most were those in which the writers have suggested we should agree on a five-year experiment which would retain the death penalty for treason, the double offender, and certainly for a man who shoots an officer while he is performing his duties.
Brutality is definitely a nasty word, and I think we should do everything in the world to get away from it. However, such a bill as this should not have its fate decided merely upon the thinking and opinions of ordinary laymen like myself. I realize it is my duty to assume my responsibility in voting upon any question that comes before this house, but I believe this issue deserves the leadership of this government. I am hoping, as other members have mentioned, that we will at least hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer). According to rumours, although rumours are sometimes false, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General are at odds concerning this bill. One will be proved to be wrong and the other right, and at least for once there is going to be one member of the treasury benches who has the right opinion concerning a bill brought before this house.
I was talking to an officer in the Salvation Army at Niagara Falls, one of the finest gentlemen in that organization. He said he was entirely in favour of this bill brought in by Mr. McGee. He said he based his opinion on the fact that not long ago he had to

spend the last six or seven hours with a man who was condemned to be hanged. He said, "Never again would I want to go through that." Then, too, perhaps I am more impressed with this bill because of the fact that as a young fellow I was only a short distance away from President McKinley when he was shot at the Pan-American exposition at Buffalo. Naturally, I have never forgotten that experience and I, like the rest of the people, would have liked to join in a riot against the murderer of that great president.
We now have to consider a revision of these attitudes which alternate between indifference and excitement and substitute therefor a dispassionate study of the lessons to be derived from the experience of other countries in which the death penalty has been abolished. We must review our own position in the light of present day facts which must guide us in our consideration of what we should do concerning capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall limit myself to a few remarks so that other hon. members may also frankly and sincerely express their views on this bill.
Hon. members will doubtlessly remember that early in the last war, Canadian prisons were offering some of their inmates conditional release provided they joined the army.
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege, during my war service, to have under my command men from all walks of life. I liked to talk over their problems with them and looked with special interest into the problems of habitual offenders, because I wanted to understand just why they had chosen to lead a life of crime. I am therefore able to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that most of those who did so were influenced by their family conditions or by the environment in which they had grown up, and many times by the lack of charity in our society, because they had been convicted when they were young and had to contend all their life with a criminal record. As they could not find any employment, they had chosen to lead a life of crime.
Our habitual offenders all said: "What we fear most are the lash and the gallows. Those are the things that keep us from carrying out our plans." Others even told me, to the last detail, the crimes they intended to commit when they would go back to civilian life.
I have just mentioned, Mr. Speaker, the main factors that lead some people into a life of crime. Before abolishing capital punish-

ment, would it not be better to amend the Criminal Code and make it provide for the destruction of the police records of young delinquents who improved their ways? Would it not be also preferable, before abolishing capital punishment, to try to improve our reform schools, and make our young delinquents understand that society and law enforcement authorities aim at their welfare when they try to reform them. Let us help our young people by recreation, and pursue our slum-clearance policy, and we will prevent crime.
Would it not be wiser, in order to prevent murder, to add to the sentence of all who have been convicted at least three times for robbery one stroke of the lash a year for each offence?
Be assured, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of criminals would think twice before committing armed robbery and would thus often escape the gallows.
Is it not said in chapter I of the Book of Kings: "He who is depraved is not corrected by words. If thou beatest thy son with the rod, he shall not die."
Let us obey those wise words with regard to those who habitually commit robbery and thus keep them from the gallows.
Psychiatrists contend that children must be brought up by reasoning. I share their views, but a good spanking from time to time is worth many words. Let us do the same with those who habitually commit robbery and we shall same them from the rope.
An attempt is being made here to abolish capital punishment by amending the Criminal Code. Before taking such action, we should give it serious consideration, because there are different kinds of murder. There is a great difference between a crime committed in cold blood for profit, and one committed in a moment of blind fury.
Abolition of capital punishment is advocated at a time when some men are prepared to blow up aircraft carrying 30, 40 or 50 people.
There is a desire to abolish capital punishment when killers, hired for a few hundred dollars, are willing to rub out any designated victim. I believe that in America the underworld is too well organized for us to even consider abolishing the death sentence.
What do you think of those young hoodlums who are addicted to narcotics and who, every day, threaten decent people with weapons of all kinds?
If we abolish capital punishment, they will kill for sport alone, and then the state will keep them all their lives in a deluxe cell.
Capital Punishment
Do you believe that the guards and even wardens of our jails would be safe? Those offenders would gladly kill their keepers just to be considered heroes among the underworld.
Some people say that according to the principles of the Christian faith killing is prohibited because the Lord said: "Thou shalt not kill". Some also argue that Cain was the first murderer and that God did not mete out death unto him. It is true; but later, when He came on earth, God gave authority, as shown in St. Paul's epistle to the Romans, chapter 13, verses 1 to 6.
Let every soul be subject onto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same: For he is the minister of God to thee for good. For if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: For he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake.
There, Mr. Speaker, the authority of human justice is set out for all to read. Justice has the power of life and death.
For those who take the liberty of falsely interpreting the Scriptures or who are opposed to capital punishment in the name of ethics, I shall quote here a very timely statement of the Canadian bishops in which no definite stand is taken for or against capital punishment:
The state has a right to condemn to death and the state has the right, even the obligation and the duty, to take appropriate measures for the efficient protection of the life of its citizens and respect for the right.
I feel therefore that we should maintain capital punishment. Let us abolish death by hanging if you wish. Let us adopt a more humane method and establish a difference between premeditated murder and crimes of passion.
Let us provide a deterrent to murder by ordering the lash for aggravated theft and revise our legislation in favour of our juvenile delinquents; if we help society to prevent crime, fifty years from now we could consider doing away with capital punishment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1955-56, a joint committee of both houses made a close study of capital punishment, corporal punishment and sweepstakes. During 45 of its 73 sittings, it

Capital Punishment
went into all aspects of capital puishment and, in its report of July 1956, I find in section 63 the following recommendation:
While the committee considered that capital punishment should be subjected to periodic review by parliament, it recommends that the death penalty should be retained as the mandatory punishment for the crime of murder.
That committee heard experts, specialists, psychiatrists and jurists give their views on all aspects of capital punishment, and it seems that the report met with the approval of the general public. And, if my memory serves me right, nothing more was said about it between 1956 and 1958. However, in the last two years, a new stand, on the part of the government, on capital punishment has again brought this problem to the fore. Indeed this debate is the result of numerous commutations by the cabinet, in accordance with the royal prerogative of mercy, in connection with death sentences pronounced by our courts. I should like to make myself quite clear on this point. I am not criticizing the cabinet for exercising the royal prerogative in cases where it considered it proper to do so. In fact, last summer, I myself, as a lawyer submitted a request for commutation of sentence to the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Balcer).
But I must say that the systematic exercise of royal prerogative by the cabinet, which commuted to life imprisonment death sentences pronounced by our courts, places us today in a paradoxical situation and, at this time, the following question comes to my mind: After the joint committee of both houses had recommended the maintenance of capital punishment, adding that the matter should be periodically reviewed by parliament, why did the government not take the initiative of introducing a bill, if it had come to the conclusion that greater clemency should be exercised in favour of accused found guilty of murder and condemned to death?
In other words, if, in the last two years, the government has adopted, a new approach to this matter, I think the purposes of justice would have been better served through some amendment to the law, in parliament, rather than through orders in council.
Mr. Speaker, I said a moment ago that we were in a paradoxical situation. That is quite evident, for at this very moment when we are discussing this bill, we have in Canada partial abolition of capital punishment, but without parliament having had anything to

do with it, contrary to the recommendation of the joint committee of both houses, whose report was submitted in July 1956.
Besides, this statement can easily be proved, since there is already a precedent, and it is no longer possible now to back down. In fact, if tomorrow, before any court of Canada, an accused were found guilty of murder and condemned to death, and if the circumstances of his murder were similar to any one of those cases where cabinet thought it proper to commute the sentence, the cabinet could not refuse commutation of the death sentence, because what is good for one must also be good for the other. This, I think, is the very essence of justice.
I therefore submit that, for the good administration of justice, the government should introduce in parliament a bill confirming the new approach it has adopted for the last two years on the matter of capital punishment.
And this brings me to the question raised by the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee). Should we abolish capital punishment?
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the abolition of capital punishment in all cases of murder where circumstances of the crime are similar to those of cases where royal mercy has been exercised by the government, but I believe we should keep on our statute books the death sentence for crimes that are particularly revolting and odious. Several of the previous speakers referred to the case of that devilish plot which, a few years ago, near Quebec, resulted in the explosion of a flying aircraft, causing the death of about fifty persons. That was a deliberate crime, whose execution, no doubt, required a very well conceived plan, and perhaps a few months' preparation. In such a case, I cannot possibly conceive that our statutes should not include some provisions which would be in keeping with the enormity of the crime.
Therefore, I favour the maintenance of capital punishment for heinous and revolting crimes of the type I have just mentioned.
As for all other murder cases where there are extenuating circumstances in favour of the accused, I think that we have reached a point today where we should give further careful consideration to this whole question. In those cases, I would be in favour of a life sentence.
In view of the many commutations the cabinet saw fit to grant in the last two years,

I submit it is imperative that the government introduce before parliament, as soon as possible, a bill to amend section 206 of the Criminal Code and, instead of trying to find a new definition of murder, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), with the help of his advisers, might consider the possibility of leaving the judge free to inflict the death penalty or a life sentence, according to the gravity and the circumstances of the crime.
Mr. Speaker, I shall therefore have to vote against the bill, because I am in favour of only partial abolition of the death penalty (Text):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all commend the sponsor of this bill for bringing this all-important matter of capital punishment to the attention of this house where it is receiving a full dress debate, as indeed it ought to. I can readily visualize how the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) was prodded by his conscience due to his own past close experiences with offences involving capital punishment. There may also even be in his subconscious mind reflections of his famed ancestor, a father of confederation and great Canadian statesman who fell at the stroke of an axe.
That this matter should be brought before this house is indeed fitting, and it is also fitting that this particular question has stirred the greatest interest of any issue placed before the public in many years. I think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was well advised when he said that everyone who by his own conscience wishes to express his ideas on the subject should be given an opportunity.
Like the hon. member for York-Scarbor-ough, I think murder is certainly a ghoulish thing. It is something which is revolting and I also think that the whole matter of capital punishment may perhaps be categorized in the same way. Everything connected with capital punishment is revolting to the common standards of decency. From the moment when the trial judge dons his tricorne black hat and pronounces the awful words that signify death to the accused standing at the bar, right until the moment when the accused does pay the supreme penalty to society, it is a succession of anguish for the criminal awaiting death. Certainly it is something that cannot be faced lightly by any normal man. It is a ghastly business. But although hanging is a ghastly business, I say there is something still more ghastly and that is premeditated and foul murder with malice aforethought.
Capital Punishment
That is why I have probed by own conscience. I did not even know what stand I should take on this issue. I thought it was common, human decency to give the man who has committed the crime of murder another chance, not to make him pay the supreme penalty. At the same time I could not help thinking that the thought of what awaits the man who dares commit murder is a powerful deterrent to him. That is why I must oppose the present bill.
This fear of having to give up one's life is not something new. Shakespeare, that great immortal interpreter of human sentiments, once wrote something along those lines:
To die, to sleep:
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub; For in that sleep of death what dreams may come When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, Must give us pause.
Those are the important words-
Must give us pause.
Must give pause, too, to the intending murderer. However, it must be remembered that capital punishment is not a deterrent to the criminal who lives in a distorted, twisted world of his own, nor can it be a deterrent to people who under intense provocation use violence on the spur of the moment which results in the death of their victims.
Nevertheless, capital punishment is a deterrent to those who premeditate their crimes, to those whose crafty minds calculate what possible gain or lucre may result from their actions. I said "crafty" and I mean crafty, because these are the people who weigh in the balance the likely advantages of their crime against the possibility of the death sentence if they are found out. If such people believe they can commit murder without being detected they are likely to do so, and that is the reason why capital punishment should be retained as a deterrent to such actions.

But how many hon. members who are listening to me here can say, consulting their own consciences, that if such a bill as this becomes law some murders which otherwise might not have been committed may be committed? I do not pretend to say that everything in the present law concerning murder, capital punishment and the rehabilitation of prisoners is right. There is a need for reform. Experts are constantly studying this field. Certainly in the case of psychopaths and in the case of a man who kills under intense provocation, capital punishment should not be imposed. Nor, in my opinion, should capital punishment be imposed in any case where conviction may have been due to judicial error. In other words, I should like to see as a part of the law of the land a certain section in our criminal legislation to the effect that a board should be empowered to review all cases and be obliged by statute to remit capital punishment in every case where there was the slightest doubt. That is going further than what the jury has to decide, because a jury must decide whether or not there is guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. I say that the role of such a board of review-and this is only a suggestion-should be to commute the sentence in every case where there was the slightest doubt that an innocent man might die.

That may be so, but I do not think that at present the regulations or the statutes are explicit enough in this particular matter.
The bill also has a wider implication than that of the deterrent effect of capital punishment. There is also the question whether or not we are living in a society where the individual has responsibility. Surely we cannot say that all people who commit crimes are sick people. There will still remain a distinction between right and wrong and, surely, a man in his sound mind knows when he is

committing a murder that he is doing something wrong. He is, perhaps, accepting the chance of being found guilty and of paying the supreme penalty.
If we abandon this principle of the responsibility of the individual who commits a murder we may as well abandon it with respect to any crime and, indeed, with respect to any person who has a job to do and who feels it is perhaps more comfortable not to do that job and who may then commit crimes of omission. Once the responsibility of the individual is remitted there is no standard upon which to guide the progress of society. That is why we should hesitate before giving this bill the force of law.
It is all very well to say: this is the trend of the times; our way of life has become softer; violence is a reversion. These are all nice words. We are proud of our society and of its progress, but we should not forget that this line of reasoning has led to what society is today, a society where we have invented the nuclear bomb. This may be the end to which this whole line of reasoning has led. It is a frightening thought that society can today only continue to exist while facing the prospect of destruction by massive atomic weapons. Yet that is the situation which faces the world today. It may have arisen because we have got away from basic principles and because there is confusion in our thinking regarding right and wrong and concerning man as a responsible person, which is the distinguishing mark of man as compared with the other creatures of this earth.
In conclusion, I can only say that I hate hanging. But even more do I hate murder, and I think this parliament should have no brief for the man who murders foully, with premeditation and with the full knowledge of all the consequences in his own perverted mind. For this reason I think all hon. members should oppose this measure and I, for one, intend to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now being considered is extremely important. We have to decide whether we should maintain capital punishment for the man who takes another man's life, or try to rehabilitate him, knowing that this attempt of rehabilitation involves many risks.
Most hon. members know that a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate studied that question in 1954 and 1955 and made a final report on its findings in 1956.

Many of the previous speakers have looked up that report and extracted from it arguments either in favour or against abolition of capital punishment.
The report stated in its findings that capital punishment should be maintained but that we should change its method of application.
Since this bill was introduced in the house by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), it was given much publicity in the newspapers, on radio and on television, so that we had a chance to find out how the man in the street reacted to it.
Most of my constituents and of other people I have talked to are against this measure because they feel it is premature. They argue that a man who takes another man's life deserves to lose his own. In pursuing conversations with these people, I had the impression that they feel the matter should receive further consideration and, therefore, that they are not prepared to support this bill.
The mover of this bill has stated his arguments in favour of his proposal. His first reason is that "capital punishment is not an effective deterrent and certainly not a unique deterrent". I quite agree, it is not a unique deterrent, but that is a far cry from saying that it is not an effective deterrent. Often, in the course of my legal practice, young men involved in conspiracies to commit break-ins, simple thefts or armed robberies, have told me that some of their friends had refused to join them for the simple reason that some of them were carrying a gun, something which often leads to murder. They were prevented from taking part in that kind of conspiracy through fear of the serious consequences of such a crime.
Moreover, the committee that studied this matter, after hearing sociologists, psychiatrists, criminologists and experts in this field, concluded that: "Capital punishment is an effective deterrent to crime, a result which neither imprisonment nor other punishments can give".
Another reason put forward by the mover of this bill is that capital punishment is based on vengeance and retribution.
Society has no vengeance to exercise against anyone. Capital punishment gained approval as a punishment, not because of a desire to exercise vengeance, but as an indication of society's disapproval for this type of crime.
The general feeling is that everyone looks upon murder with horror. We were told of the feelings of a prisoner condemned to the gallows, but we must not forget the
Capital Punishment
feelings of the victim and of his family. What about the children who are left fatherless because of some atrocious crime? What are the consequences for the future of these children who are deprived of their father, of their support? Who knows, perhaps the future of the family may be jeopardized forever.
Another reason put forward is the possibility of judicial error. I have attended several murder trials, and have always been impressed with the many precautions taken in conducting that kind of trial. The presiding judge has no prejudice against the accused; as far as he is concerned, it is just another case, and the whole procedure follows the requirements of the Criminal Code. Jurors are selected with utmost care and are questioned with regard to their views on capital punishment; they are asked whether they already have an opinion on the case, or whether they have other views that might cause prejudice to the accused; moreover, they can at any time be rejected by the defence.
It is the responsibility of the presiding judge to explain the law to the jury, to comment on the facts without expressing an opinion, and this is always done.
Besides, the accused is always given the benefit of the doubt; and if he thinks he is being wronged, he can always appeal and have his first trial reviewed by another court. The whole trial is then reviewed by the Department of Justice and the governor in council may, by royal prerogative, grant a commutation of sentence. As can be seen, Mr. Speaker, the right of the accused is well respected by his peers.
I believe that our penal system is perfect in that regard and that the accused is treated fairly. However, like previous speakers, I think that hanging is antiquated, gruesome and altogether objectionable. I suggest that our Criminal Code should be amended to provide some other method of execution.
Mr. Speaker, I will vote against this bill, because I believe that we should maintain capital punishment, not in a spirit of revenge on the part of society, but as a deterrent to other crimes.
