subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Commons debate on capital punishment for the crime of murder is now in its second day. We now know that the debate will terminate in a division, that the division bells will soon ring out their clamorous call



Capital Punishment
through the corridors of this building summoning us to come to the house and vote. How shall we vote? We are divided in this house. In the cities, towns and hamlets of Canada, across the miles of our beloved land, from ocean to furious ocean, our people await the decision that will follow the ringing of the division bells.
Before we vote may one man speak quietly for man? What are we deciding? Is man incorruptible? Is man perfect? Is he perfectible? Is man everlastingly the keeper of his brother? If he is not, and if the heart, mind and body are sometimes used in such a way that man is a little less than the angels, shall we who are made in same image take judgment upon the one temporal thing that makes man different from the animal and defines him as an individual, consciousness and life?
In the quiet places I think all of us have thought as deeply as we can about this question. We should have a melting for man. Hear the words of a very great man, Albert Schweitzer, who said:
For months on end I lived in a continual state of mental excitement. Without the least success I let my thinking be concentrated, even all through my daily work at the hospital, on the real nature of the affirmative attitude and of ethics, and on the question of what they have in common. ... I was staying with my wife on the coast at cape Lopez for the sake of her health-it was in September, 1915-when I was summoned to visit Madame Pelot, the ailing wife of a missionary ... about 160 miles upstream. The only means of conveyance I could find was a small steamer, towing an overladen barge, which was on the point of starting. Except myself, there were only natives on board, but among them was Emil Ogouma, my friend from Lambarene. Since I had been in too much of a hurry to provide myself with enough food for the journey, they let me share the contents of their cooking pot. Slowly we crept upstream, laboriously feeling... for the channels between the sandbanks. Lost in thought I sat on the deck of the barge, struggling to find the elementary and universal conception of the ethical which I had not discovered in any philosophy. Sheet after sheet I covered with disconnected sentences, merely to keep myself concentrated on the problem. Late on the third day, at the very moment when, at sunset, we were making our way through a herd of hippopotamuses, there flashed upon my mind, unforseen and unsought, the phrase, "Reverence for Life." The iron door had yielded: the path in the thicket had become visible.
Many of us want the death penalty abolished for the crime of murder. We want it abolished because in the hands of the state calculatedly to take an individual human life seems to us to defy reverence for life and reverence for life is the whole essence of man. The retentionists among us, for whose views and opinions we have wide respect, argue that after all murderers have no reverence for life and therefore the state ought to be guided by a similar code. What shall we say to this argument-that it tries

to recompense the private, individual and wrongful taking of life by a public, calculated, scheduled taking of life by the state. If the taking of life is the essence, on what shifty ground do we stand if we decide that what is wrong for the individual becomes right for the state?
In this house as in our land there are men and women of many creeds and many faiths. We all agree on one thing, that in a society such as ours which attests to any spiritual purpose, if there is any reason for life in a society with any concept of spiritual faith, then the state must be governed by the same moral imperatives that govern the individual. Man is not perfectible; man is not perfect. But the retentionists throughout the debate have failed to establish the one base upon which their case could be proven, and that is that capital punishment for the crime of murder is a unique deterrent.
My faith teaches me that the state possesses the authority from God to take the life of a criminal only when such a penalty is necessary to preserve the common good of all. If it should be discovered that long imprisonment serves equally well in deterring crime then the death penalty would have to be abolished, for as soon as the need for it ceases the state no longer possesses God's authority to use it.
Earlier today in this debate it was said by one of those who support the retention of capital punishment for the crime of murder that the drive to end capital punishment was typical of certain degenerate and dangerous ideas current in this century and especially on this continent. Is it degenerate to preach mercy? Capital punishment is punitive, purgative and primitive. When we vote in this house we ourselves will be deciding whether we shall be the hangman, for if we retain capital punishment after a long and public debate on it then every man who goes to the gallows, every many who dies at the hands of the state, shall have his fate conferred upon him by the members of the house. We are indeed making ourselves the hangman if we retain capital punishment.
I do not say this in any terrifying way, but it is in our hands to take away the death penalty for the crime of murder and I am one of those who believe that it should be taken away. I do not believe that the state has the right or should act out the right calculatedly to do that which is wrong when done by an individual, and unless it can be proved that capital punishment is a unique deterrent-and it cannot be proven-then the reason for the retention of the death penalty is abolished. The state would then no longer possess God's authority to use it.


In ancient days men used to place thousands of their fellow men in arenas for a classic blood bath. Convicted and unconvicted alike were subjected to primitive forms of the death penalty, being dragged along by chariot, staked out, burned. In our century we have come to hanging and then to the gas chamber and electrocution. We do it all in the still of the night so as to conceal our shame.
The essence of the argument for the death penalty for the crime of murder is human life. This is what defines the question before us. Man is different because he is possessed of some spark of divinity. We ought not to take into our own hands the capacity to snuff out that divinity.
Our police, our protective staffs and their families, the families and relatives of the victims of past murders, are naturally concerned. We all have a great sympathy for their concern. But to say that the death penalty should be retained to provide protection for them, I believe to be illogical, because surely we are condemning our protective system. Surely, we can arrive at some way of giving assurance to these people without exacting the death penalty.
My whole case, both in the debate during this session and the debate during the last session for the elimination of the death penalty for the crime of murder is based upon my conception of man. Man is different because he possesses divine life. We ought not, calculatedly, to take it from him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
I have
listened, Mr. Speaker, with extreme interest to the views which have been expressed so far. I, for one, and I am sure each member of the house as well as the people of the country are pleased that the debate has followed the lines suggested by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) when he introduced the bill and suggested the debate should not be politically partisan, but should be one in which each member reflected his own inner thoughts on the subject. This, of course, is not to indicate that if a political party wants of itself to make a determination on this question, that is not quite all right.
However, I think the tenor of the debate, following the suggestion by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, will be most conducive to a truer reflection of the feelings of the members of this house when we do get a vote on this bill than would have been the case if the discussion had been carried on on a political basis. I should like to express my congratulations to the hon. member for York-Scarborough upon his introduction and also, I am sure, express the appreciation of hon. members of this house who have been interested in this subject for more years than
Capital Punishment
I have in seeing this particular issue proceed to the stage it has already reached because we may finally be able to express ourselves by means of a vote. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who has been a proponent of this idea for many years, and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney), who also made an excellent contribution, are happy to see that we are reaching a stage when we might be making a definite decision one way or the other.
There has been a bit of discussion about public opinion, and whether public opinion as it is assessed by the individual member should have a great influence on the actions or attitudes of individual members. I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), who I do not think is here at the moment, and the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), dealt with this question to some extent and used it as the basis of their attitude at that time. I am afraid, that neither one of the hon. gentlemen would know what public opinion was if it came right up and smacked them in the eye, especially on this particular issue. We all know that public opinion on the question of capital punishment fluctuates from region to region, depending on the circumstances.
For example, if a person with a perverted mind makes a sexual attack upon a young child and, in the process, this young child is killed, public opinion in that particular area will become quite definitely in favour of capital punishment for a certain length of time because the circumstances surrounding that particular death are such that they influence public opinion in that area. Public opinion is divided, is an expression used sometimes. Some are in favour of the bill before us and some are against it. Opinion in this house is divided. I think this will always be so. I do not think we will find, on this particular issue of capital punishment or on any other issue, that public opinion is solidly one way or the other. There will be this division of attitude throughout the country, just as there is on many of the other bills before this house.
I would say in this case that hon. members-I say this without disrespect to their constituents or to the public-should probably be less sensitive to public opinion than they are at other times. I think that public opinion, because it can fluctuate, because it can be influenced by the circumstances surrounding a particular murder, could, if it were followed, have the same effect upon the members of this house as politics had upon the capital punishment question in New Zealand. We might find ourselves, at one stage, in a fairly relaxed mood agreeing to

Capital Punishment
the abolition of capital punishment. Shortly thereafter there might be one or two very cruel, bizarre murders take place, with all the gruesome things that attend upon such murders, and this would influence the members of the house another way. We would find ourselves oscillating between being in favour and being against the abolition of capital punishment. I think we are much better advised, as I say, to be less sensitive to public opinion and more sensitive to our own consciences; let them be our guide.
It is a well known fact, especially to the hon. member for Parkdale, that the facts are incontrovertible in so far as the death penalty being more of a deterrent than, say, life imprisonment. One is not any more of a deterrent force than the other. The great majority-this is from memory more than any reference to the statistical information contained in the proceedings of the joint committee which investigated this question a few years ago-of homicides or murders that were committed were committed as a result of emotion or passion. In those cases, certainly the threat or the possibility of capital punishment was not a deterrent, it was not even a factor. It will not be a factor when emotions are involved. A criminal, for instance, in the act of robbing a bank or breaking into a building will not be deterred from avoiding apprehension by the police by the thought of capital punishment. He will not be deterred from taking action against the police officer or anyone else who may participate in his apprehension. Not only is capital punishment not a deterrent, it is not even a factor.
The major factor involved is that a person who is caught in the midst of a crime is going to do whatever he can to prevent himself from being caught, to prevent himself from being captured or taken to jail. He wants to get away. He does not want the policeman to arrest him and he will use whatever means are at his disposal, arising out of some emotional feeling, to avoid being arrested or to prevent himself from being arrested and in the process may commit a homicide or murder.
There is the question of premeditated murder. I know we all look with as much abhorrence as we can upon the type of murder that is committed by premeditation where the lives of people other than the intended victim are involved, such as in the placing on an airplane of a bomb that in the process not only kills the intended victim but 30, 40 or 50 other people besides, as in the instance referred to a few moment ago.
In this case it is possible that this premeditated murder arises out of two reasons. One is mental unbalance or lack of mental

balance of the person who is committing that premeditated crime or is premeditating the commission of murder. The other is that the individual is in fairly good control of his faculties, knows what the consequences will be if he is apprehended but is willing to pit his ability and his intelligence against the forces of society which might detect him in the process of the murder he is about to commit.
If a person such as that placed in a plane a bomb that killed his intended victim so that he could reap the rewards, whether they be insurance benefits or otherwise, and he did it out of a mental unbalance or insanity, then capital punishment was not a deterrent in that case or even a factor. If he did it in full control of his faculties, being willing to pit his ability to commit the crime against the abilities of the police force, then capital punishment was not a deterrent in that case and in fact was not a factor. The only factor is that the individual knows that if he is apprehended he is going to be hanged just the same as he knows that if he is apprehended he might receive life imprisonment. In those cases, regardless of the opinions expressed by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), there is no balanced reasoning to say that capital punishment is a deterrent. Certainly in those three or four instances I have outlined it is not a deterrent. It could not even be a factor in those cases. In others it is no more of a deterrent than is the threat of life imprisonment.
The hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue indicated that by the retention of the present statute we are sure there will be no increase in the number of murders that are committed but that if we vote in favour of this bill and support it, we are not sure whether or not there will be an increase. Of course the hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue, experienced as he might be, does not know that at all. It is a belief that he has. He believes that there will be no increase as long as we retain the present statute. But statistics in other countries were mentioned. I think some 40 jurisdictions were mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdale where this question has been studied quite thoroughly. They indicate, as any hon. member can agree and, in fact, I think will agree, that there are many other factors affecting the rate of murder far more than does this question of capital punishment.
There is the question of the judge and the court making an error. As I understand it, there is not a clear case in Canada where a person has been hanged for murder and where subsequent events have proved that he was

the wrong person although there are cases in which grave doubt has been expressed as to whether the person hanged actually committed the crime.
Professor Borchard of Yale wrote a book called "Conviction of the Innocent" in which he makes a study of some 65 United Kingdom and United States cases, 25 of which involved murder and all of which, including the 25 which involved murder, indicated that the individual accused was initially found guilty and sentenced but that subsequent events proved that this sentence was in error and that the person in fact was not guilty either because of mistaken identity and perjury, circumstantial evidence or a combination of those factors or other factors, and that in those cases an error had been made.
There is one case in Canada, that of Mr. Wilbur Coffin-quite a prominent case a few years ago-who was hanged and about which very grave doubts were expressed as to his guilt. Nevertheless, the individual was hanged regardless of those doubts.
Courts have made errors in other cases in Canada; I refer not to murder cases but to other convictions. People have been sentenced to jail or to penitentiary and, after having served a period of time, subsequent events have shown those individuals were not in fact guilty of the offence of which they had been found guilty. Some of those cases involved robbery with violence. I think we are entitled to speculate upon what would have occurred if, in two instances particularly that come to mind, in the course of the robbery someone had been murdered. Then I think we are entitled to speculate that those persons who had been found guilty of that crime, if there had been a murder involved, could quite probably have been hanged for that murder; and in those two particular cases subsequent events proved, even although murder was not involved, that the people who were convicted were not guilty and they were released from the penitentiary after serving a certain period of time of the initial sentence.
Courts are not infallible. Juries are not infallible. The government, in its consideration of whether or not a case should be commuted, is not infallible. No one can say for sure that each case of murder in which a person is convicted is absolute proof that in each case the individual who was convicted was in fact the person who committed the murder. There is a chance for error. We should consider that chance for error very seriously. We should consider it in addition to the other reasons that have been given, both by myself and by many other hon. members in this house. We should consider this question of error and consider whether we are entitled
Capital Punishment
to cause an error to be made, or to allow an error to be made and thereby to inflict upon innocent wives and children-or husband and children, if it is a case of a woman -who may be left behind after an individual may well have been incorrectly or improperly or in error sentenced to death and in fact hanged.
I do not think parliament or the state has any right to place the benefit of doubt against the accused, especially in view of the fact of all of the other inconvertible evidence and facts that have been presented for the abolition of capital punishment.
In closing, if I have not indicated it already, I might as well say this now in order that it may be clear. I intend to vote in favour of the bill that is at present before us.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the explanatory notes of this bill it states:
Section 206 at present reads as follows:-
"Every one who commits murder is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be sentenced to death."
There are no qualifications. It is not a matter of whether it is premeditated, or a crime of passion which is committed on the spur of the moment; the penalty is the same.
It has been said by others that the outstanding defect of the law concerning murder is that it provides a single punishment for a crime which can vary widely in the degree of culpability. The rigidity of this law is mitigated only by the prerogative of mercy, exercised in Canada by the cabinet. In the last 40 sentences of capital punishment, the cabinet have remitted 32. In one case the judge, under the wording of this act, was forced to sentence a 14-year old boy to be hanged.
This present law-I think hon. members who have spoken for and against abolition are agreed on this-in its present state is a barbarous law, the law of the jungle, a vindictive law, a law of vengeance, and a law which is repudiated by the great majority of Canadians, a law which in fact has been declared by the action of the government to be too severe a penalty in 80 per cent of the cases.
There are at present before this house three private bills and a resolution which seeks to make changes in the section of the Criminal Code having to do with murder. Through you, Mr. Speaker, this house has ruled that this debate need not be limited to the bill immediately before us but can encompass the subject matter of these other bills. The other bills seek some practical half-way house between the existing law, under which every

Capital Punishment
person convicted of murder must be sentenced to death, and the total abolition of the death penalty.
As long as we had only one bill before the house, the one we are presently debating, the issue was clear: it was either total abolition, or the law remained as it is now. The introduction of these other bills introduces new factors, and there is nothing to stop other hon. members with other ideas introducing further bills adding further variations. This confusion will only be resolved if we pass this bill, which would then dispose of the matter once and for all. However, if this bill does not pass or if it does not come to a vote then I believe the government must take responsibility of bringing in their own legislation.
It was because of this, that I placed on the order paper a resolution in the following terms:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation this session to amend the Criminal Code in regard to capital punishment.
The debate last Thursday found at least nine speakers favouring abolition and eight against abolition; but almost all speakers, as I said before, favoured some change in the law. So far today we have had eight speakers, and there seem to be three-and here I declare myself-in favour of abolition, one, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) would like to have a five-year trial period, which has a great deal of merit in it, and four speakers are opposed.
What are the reasons for abolition? First of all, there is the moral and ethical one, that the deliberate taking of a human life is an act which no one person or the community should be able to exercise over another human being. The Belgian industry of justice in 1930, after 67 years with the death penalty in abeyance, had this to say:
The lesson has been learnt that the best means of inculcating respect for human life is to refrain from taking life in the name of the law.
Society in taking life harms itself because of the debasing and brutalizing effect on the community as a whole owing to this action.
There is of course another reason which has been touched on by many hon. members and that is the possibility of error. Capital punishment is irrevocable and no matter how rare mistakes may be they have happened, and can happen again. The Montreal Gazette of February 19 carried a news story in which a leading Montreal criminal lawyer, Mr. Raymond Daoust, had this to say. He was speaking, incidentally, to some 700 University of Montreal students, and he reported on 22 cases where persons were executed in

the last two centuries for crimes later found to have been committed by others.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart), speaking against this bill, did not think the chance of an innocent person being convicted was very great. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), for whom I have tremendous respect and admiration, can be allowed the odd mistake, but I would like to quote from his remarks reported on page 1214 of Hansard for February 18 last where he quoted Lord Chief Justice Darling of the privy council who had stated in the house of commons committee of the United Kingdom in 1930 that in his 26 years' experience on the bench he was convinced that, and I quote:
In view of the checks and safeguards of English law, it is practically impossible for an innocent man to be hanged, although a great many guilty ones escaped.
The same thought was echoed by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell). I do not propose to argue the accuracy of these statements, the one of Mr. Daoust and the one I have just quoted, but I do wish to say that for society to take the life of even one innocent person is a crime against society and a blow against our fundamental, moral and religious ideals.
The real heart of the problem is not whether capital punishment is a deterrent against committing murder, but whether it is, as the mover of the bill stated, a unique deterrent. The question is: Does the danger a criminal runs of being executed act as more of a deterrent than if the sentence were life imprisonment? If the retention of capital punishment were to prevent murders which would otherwise take place, then there would be no ground for its abolition except on purely moral grounds. However, there has been placed before the house a great deal of data about experience in states which have abolished capital punishment, and although this data does not conclusively-as I would be the first to admit, and as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) said-establish that it is not a deterrent, it certainly does not establish that it is a deterrent.
There are two types of crimes, the impulsive, that mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the crime of emotion and passion, and the premeditated crime. In the impulsive type of crime the criminal does not think of the consequences; the act is done on the spur of the moment. With regard to premeditated crimes, as has been said by other hon. members, the criminal is so convinced that he will not be brought to justice that the question whether the penalty is capital punishment or not is of no effect as far as he is concerned.

The experience of Great Britain in this matter was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary South, as reported on page 1213 of Hansard. He said that the situation in Great Britain had been outlined; Great Britain a year ago experienced a crime wave during which eight murders were committed in eight days.
If these are reasons for retention of capital punishment, then they are reasons which have the same philosophy of thinking as the presumption that if we have a 20-inch snowfall in Ottawa in three days, then in one month we will have a 200-inch snowfall. I have listened to all speakers so far, but as yet there has not been a real case made out that capital punishment is a deterrent. The record in England is a matter of fact. Indeed, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) placed it on the pages of Hansard, and I think hon. members should read this passage over and over again. I shall quote from page 1189:
Another common misconception with regard to this bill which is quoted in letters and newspapers concerns the supposed restoration of the death penalty in England. It is a fact that the death penalty was never abolished in England. It passed a free vote in the House of Commons by a small margin, and during the interval between the time it passed the house and went to the Lords the home secretary very properly deemed it advisable to commute all death sentences.
I think it is of more than passing interest while discussing England to mention some statistics which emerged from that experience. During the 18 months before the suspension period the number of murders committed were 256. The death penalty was suspended for a period of 18 months, and the number of murders during that period was 246. During the 17 months after restoration, which was the period of time which elapsed for which these figures were made available, the number of murders committed was 310.
As I said, a great deal of data has been placed on record with regard to the effect of capital punishment as a deterrent or as a non-deterrent. One can sum up the case for the retention of capital punishment as a deterrent by saying that if capital punishment prevented one murder of an innocent person it should be retained. That was the theme of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue (Mr. Martineau). I suggest that if we are to accept this as a true statement and as one to which we should pay attention, we are entitled to say that if one innocent person is saved from the gallows and escapes murder by society as a result of the abolition of the death penalty, then the death penalty should be abolished. If the argument is right on one side of the ledger it is right on the other.
I have pointed out that capital punishment provides a single penalty for crimes which may be as different as night and day. A fight may cause a death and result in a sentence 79951-0-92
Capital Punishment
of capital punishment or just as easily may result in a charge of assault and battery being laid. The intent is the same, the circumstances are the same, but the result is drastically different. A slightly heavier blow can mean this difference, or the manner in which an assaulted person may fall. As the hon. member for York-Scarborough pointed out, the difference of a fraction of an inch in the direction of a bullet can mean the difference between death and life for the victim and for the murderer.
The wisest words which have been spoken in this debate were, in my view, those which were spoken by the hon. member for Parkdale when he placed upon society a certain amount of blame before a murder actually takes place. As recorded at page 1200 of Hansard, the hon. member said this:
The death penalty Is not the answer to the problem of crime and of criminals. Crime has its cause and crime has its cure. Its causes are clear. They can be stated like the litany: they are slums, they are broken homes; they are poverty; they are drunkenness, divorce, lack of opportunity, lack of education. These are the causes of crime.
The case for the abolition of capital punishment was also stated a great many centuries ago, and I am indebted to the social action committee of the Unitarian congregation of south Peel for the following illustration. When some members of a heretical African sect confessed to murdering Christians around 400 A.D., St. Augustine wrote:
We do not wish to have the sufferings of the servants of God avenged by the infliction of precisely similar injuries in the way of retaliation. Not, of course, that we object to the removal from these wicked men of the liberty to perpetrate further crimes, but our desire is rather that justice be satisfied without the taking of their lives or the maiming of their bodies in any particular; and that by such coercive measures as may be in accordance with the laws, they be drawn away from their insane frenzy to the quietness of men in their sound judgment, or compelled to give up mischievous violence and betake themselves to some useful labour.
Whatever may be the result of this debate, one thing I know, namely that a change is taking place. A change is taking place in this house and in the country. Whether the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough passes this house or not, we shall have made some progress at least in the way we deal with convicted murderers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member where he stands in relation to the matter of life imprisonment? Does he mean it should really be for life, or that the present system, where there is commutation, should be continued?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
That is a point which I have been considering. It is an anomaly, also, because at the present time the sentence of

Capital Punishment
a murderer may be commuted, in which case it would amount to ordinary life imprisonment, whereas the present bill would mean that the whole of a man's natural life might be spent in imprisonment. Thus a person who was sentenced under this bill would receive a more severe sentence than if his death sentence had been commuted by the cabinet. However, I think these are matters of detail which will have to be sorted out by the law officers of the crown. This is partly the reason I brought in my resolution, since one bill might provide for degrees of murder; another might give a jury the power of extending mercy; and a third might say that discretion should rest with the judge. There could be many variations in the approach, but the sum and substance is that one can either abolish capital punishment or the government itself brings in a bill taking into account the debate which has been going on now for two days and which will go on for the third, in addition to expressions of public opinion in the country.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, I should like to rectify to some extent the wrong impression current among the public at large with regard to the so-called free vote. It has been said in certain quarters that, since this vote has been announced as a free vote, in other cases members were not free to vote according to their conscience.
I have said again and again, ever since I have been elected, as far back as 1935, as a member either of the Quebec legislature or of parliament, that I have always voted freely and according to my own conscience.
Caucus meetings are held by all political parties in order to help their members examine questions thoroughly. All of us at times have to fall in with the general opinion and we recognize, as intelligent men, that if the caucus majority does not share our views, either we are in the wrong, in which case we are the last ones to find out, or we are ahead of our times and we must wait for public opinion to crystallize. In either case, we freely withdraw our personal viewpoint and we invariably vote freely and according to our conscience.
Today, this debate is exactly of the kind we have in our caucuses, where each member is free to say what he thinks, in his own way, and to make his decision according to the judgment he has formed in the light of the discussion. I believe that all previous speakers and those who will follow, and even those who will not take part in this debate, have always, as I have, voted freely and according to their conscience.

Mr. Speaker, I recall that many years ago, during the first world war, a certain crisis had taken hold of the public. Good and pious people, priests, Protestant ministers, rabbis had undertaken the task of eliminating alcoholism from the face of the earth. Surely those people were the most sincere men in the world; they were well-intentioned.
They also had on their side the underworld which, for a quite different reason-that of promoting a new type of business-wanted to help them out, so both camps did their best to check alcoholism. What were the results? Alcoholism increased, the underworld made a fortune and, for the first time in history, women became accustomed to public drinking, because of the "mickey" or the small "hip" as it was then called.
Since that time, a spirit that I would describe as "Caponian" has come into being, and the underworld has established all possible kinds of institutions for the speakeasies, for the sale of narcotics, and murder has resulted.
Yet, the people who wanted this were sincere, honest and had the welfare of the population in mind; but they forgot that excess of any kind is bad. They went to extremes and fell into a worse evil.
Nowadays, a certain mood has been revived among the public. People have seized upon this idea of capital punishment, and everyone, from one end of the country to the other, is demanding either its abolition or maintenance. All of them are good, sincere and honest people; we even find among them Catholic priests, Protestant ministers, and rabbis. In other words, the best citizens of the community are asking for the abolition of capital punishment. The underworld too is asking for the abolition of capital punishment, but of course for another reason; they are requesting it, in order not to become victims of it. Communists are also requesting the abolition of capital punishment, for reasons they alone could explain.
And yet, is the idea of abolition of capital punishment a new one? No, it is a very, very old one. In the fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries in France, Voltaire and Jean-Jacques Rousseau were advocating abolition of capital punishment; in Italy, Vico and Beccaria were advocating the abolition of capital punishment; in Germany, you will recall that Savigny, Karl Marx and Kelsen were requesting the abolition of capital punishment. In the fifteenth century in England, Hume and Bentham were also requesting the abolition of capital punishment. On this side of the

Atlantic, Franklin and Paine spent their life asking for the abolition of capital punishment.
This discussion is only a repetition of all those that have taken place since that time. And what are the reasons advanced? For some, it is a question of conscience, because they maintain that we have no right to kill our fellow man, that the state has no right to kill, because the commandment says; "Thou shalt not kill".
But, if we accept the teachings of the bible-I have here the Catholic bible, which I compared with the King James version, and they are in every way the same-we find in Genesis, chapter 9, verse 6:
Who so sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed-
It is not said that his blood will be shed by the grace of God only but:
-by man shall his blood be shed.
Could we therefore hold that any individual could shed the blood of another out of revenge, or punish the one who has killed another man? This means the state, as it was constituted at that time, a patriarchal state, and the head of that state had the right to render justice in the name of the state.
And, further on, if we look up Leviticus chapter 24, verse 17, we find this:
And he that killeth any man shall surely be nut to death-
Also, further on in the bible, in Numbers, chapter 25, verses 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20- about he who strikes to kill-we find this:
And if he smite him with an instrument of iron, so that he die, he is a murderer: the murderer shall surely be put to death. And if he smite him with throwing a stone, wherewith he may die, and he die, he is a murderer: the murderer shall surely be put to death. Or if he smite him with an hand weapon of wood, wherewith he may die, and he die, he is a murderer: the murderer shall surely be put to death.

Mr. Speaker, when I had to interrupt my remarks at six o'clock, I was telling conscientious objectors that they could very well base their faith on the teachings of the bible, that inspired book, to promote the maintenance of capital punishment.
79951-0-92J
Capital Punishment
We also see in chapter 35, verse 20, the following:
But if he thrust him of hatred, or hurl at him by laying of wait, that he die; or in enmity smite him with his hand, that he die: he that smote him shall surely be put to death; for he is a murderer:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there must be premeditation. That is provided in our laws.
No one can be condemned unless there has been premeditation. Now, if we examine the judgments rendered in the last few years, we note a tendency not to condemn those who could have killed either by accident, or under the impulse of a sudden access of violence, which could then have prevented them from being in full possession of their faculties.
The bible goes even further. It refers to evidence.
We see, for instance, in Deuteronomy, chapter 19, verses 18 and 19, the following:
And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother; then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother: so shalt thou put the evil away from among you.
The bible goes so far as to be as severe with regard to the false witness as it is with the murderer.
This is similar to what the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) said a few moments ago.
Indeed, the bible tells us that there should be two witnesses, not one only, to bring about a conviction. No conviction can be based on a single testimony.
Consequently, the conscientious objector finds, I think, enough explanation in the bible for continuing the Lord's work, i.e.: to condemn him who causes his brother's death.
Mr. Speaker, we may be looked upon as barbarians, if we continue to apply capital punishment. But what about the murderer? It is claimed that those who would maintain capital punishment have outmoded views on civilization. But people seem to forget that it is the murderer himself who has acted like a barbarian. People completely overlook the victim, who was eliminated from the world, and who might have continued living a useful life, to think only of the poor murderer who will soon be dangling at the end of a rope.
I think that is pushing sentimentalism too far. We have not the right to be too concerned over the fate of the murderer.
1460	HOUSE OF
Capital Punishment
It is claimed that this is an act of vengeance. How can it be? It is an act of retribution.
As a matter of fact, it is not the state which does the convicting, it is the criminal who convicts himself. A criminal knows that if he kills, he will suffer the death penalty. What does the state do? The state, through its courts, tries to establish the truth, or to point up the facts indicating whether the accused is guilty or not.
Indeed, under our judicial system, the duty of the crown attorney is not to try to win a case, but to try to prove, on a factual basis, whether the accused is guilty or not guilty.
Now if the accused has been found guilty, he himself decrees his death sentence by committing what he had no right to commit. We must therefore ignore the claim that the state acted in a spirit of vengeance.
It has also been claimed that capital punishment is no deterrent to crime. I think this is quite difficult to prove with figures, because statistics have not been established long enough, neither in the states which abolished the death penalty, nor in those where it is maintained, for us to be able to state in a final way that capital punishment is a deterrent to crime.
There is, however, a really surprising thing. It has been said that under Napoleon, at a certain time, and more particularly after the battle of Russia, several officers committed suicide. Napoleon, who was a psychologist, then decreed that all who would commit suicide would hang. Now, do you know that from then on, suicides stopped, because officers did not want their families' name to be tarnished because of their being sentenced to hang. If such action in Napoleon's time put a stop to a wave of suicide, it is quite clear that capital punishment may incite others, who are not hardened criminals, to spare their families the shame which their sentence to the gallows would bring upon them.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it may not be due to that so much as to a softening of our way of life, but there have been more sentences commuted for the last two years than ever before. However, if we examine relevant statistics, we will find that, for the past two years, criminality has rapidly increased. Could it be that people are saying: "there is no more danger, we have every chance in the world to have our sentence commuted"?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not only in favour of maintaining capital punishment,


but in favour of hanging. I do not like the gas chamber, precisely because of what is happening in this country now. Everybody is worried at the thought of the rope. Well, as long as there is a means of worrying people at the thought of the gallows, it will be a deterrent to those who mean to kill.
Capital punishment obliterates a social evil in the person of those who refuse to obey the law. Indeed, the greatest social evil is perhaps not that which is punished by death. The greatest evil, for which I think we are perhaps responsible, is the fact that children are left to grow up with all their faults. We are afraid to correct them in the good old way, like most hon. members here and myself have been. Indeed, there are some of them who would benefit by being corrected again.
It is said in the book of Proverbs-which is also in the bible-that:
Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that again is a word of truth, coming from a book of truth that has been given to man, through the light of the Holy Ghost.
It is said in the bible that children must be corrected. Besides, that is not new. We know that if a tree has a tendency to grow crooked when it is young, if we straighten it, if we take care of it, we can succeed in having it grow straight, and have a tree that will be of real value.
It should be the same for children; but, unfortunately, in our modern society, there are people who would like to have religious instruction removed from our schools, and it is with the help of religious convictions that we will better succeed in protecting children from all those miseries which incline them to do all sorts of stupid things.
It seems to be the belief, in some quarters, that religious instruction should be left to the church and the home. Well, if we had carried on that religious instruction, if we had impressed on those young minds the teachings we find in the sacred books, I am sure there would not be so much juvenile crime.
Nowadays, some people would like to replace that correction system which used to reform children. They would like to replace it by psychological methods. There are so many psychologists in the world today, that a certain thinker said a few years ago: "A

world that has so many psychologists and psychiatrists must be very ill indeed". I think this world is very ill indeed, because it is forgetting the only good method of overcoming the evil which exists at present.
Mr. Speaker, society has its responsibility, but it is not by abolishing capital punishment that we will succeed in eradicating that evil. First of all, we should start by the beginning. Before abolishing capital punishment, we should first give consideration to changing our whole penal system. We should make a complete study of it, and once we have found means to properly punish those who have committed offences or crimes, then we will perhaps be in a position to consider abolishing that practice.
At present, there are people condemned to life imprisonment who, after 10, 12 or 15 years, are released.
If a young man of twenty commits a murder and is condemned to life imprisonment, he is sometimes released after 15 years, that is at the age of 35 years.
As regards the one who commits an armed robbery in a bank and who, when a nervous clerk (who is doing a service to society), steps back in his cage, draws his weapon and kills him, if he is not sentenced to death, he deserves to be made to witness every execution so that he will know what hanging is like. Furthermore, not only should we not abolish the death penalty, but we should also extend it to other crimes. I submit for instance that whoever rapes a child under twelve, deserves hanging even more than does a murderer. The men higher up among peddlers of narcotics, the organizers of the drug traffic, who do not touch the stuff but find others to push the product, those who spread that bad habit among the public at large are more guilty than all murderers. I say that they should be sentenced to death although there is no such provision in the Criminal Code.
I submit that it should be possible to revise our Criminal Code and to come back later on that matter, but not today, because we are not ready to accept the abolition of the death penalty, and consequently I shall vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) has triggered a debate during which a number of hon. members spoke with both knowledge and ability.
Capital Punishment
Having been a member of the Quebec bar for close to 33 years, and having acted in a number of trials for murder some times as crown attorney, some times as attorney for the defence, and having constantly looked for the instincts and psychological motives which, in the last resort, were at the basis of the murder, I have acquired an experience I had never sought, and from which I have occasionally tried to draw some conclusions. That is what prompts me to make this modest contribution to an important debate. I shall try to show the same objective and unbiased attitude as the hon. members who spoke before me.
The death penalty, which is the first and most ancient penalty ever inflicted by mankind, has always been one of man's major concerns.
Throughout history, philosophers, moralists, sociologists and lawyers either denounced it as a barbarous act, or proclaimed it as a social necessity.
Some have claimed that the murderer is just irresponsible, either because of his mental state or of a natural weakness, or again because of the environment in which he has lived and grown, and that consequently, justice is always too harsh on him.
Others say: men are different from one another, and generalizations in such matters go against common sense and against the truth. Every man enjoys a certain degree of conscience and willpower, which enable him to choose his own course and which make him responsible for his actions. Every man must remain within the framework of social order, and if he transgresses that order, society has to protect itself against him. And proponents of that theory add: those criminals, who have felt no pity, will feel no remorse. They have shown no respect for human life, yet they expect society to respect their own, despite the fact that they are a danger. How can they be stopped from committing further crimes? Is there some means of frightening those who might be tempted to follow in their footsteps and threaten the life of peaceful citizens, which the state has a duty to protect? Nature and mankind in the past have replied by applying the death penalty.
Such is the dilemma inherent in the problem now before us. To find the perfect solution, one would have to be the creator of man, or have acquired a complete and absolute knowledge of man. One would have to know in detail the mechanics of his thoughts and motivations, and be able to ex-

Capital Punishment
plain each and every one of his moves. However, the science of man is the least developed of all sciences, and one of the greatest minds of our time, who published the results of 20 years of research in a famous book, found no more appropriate title than this: Man, the Unknown.
Ignorance however should not be an excuse for not seeking the answer to all the problems concerning the protection of the public, which is the main duty of every state. One undeniable principle is that every individual is a personalized being endowed with intelligence and free will, a being who ultimately-and I mean a normal man-decides for himself what he does or refrains from doing. That is the basis of responsibility.
On the other hand, the state has the strict obligation to keep order and to safeguard peace and security for citizens who respect its authority and its laws. Thence, its right to punish, to the extent of their responsibility and guilt, those who flout those rules, and justice makes it an obligation for the state to establish some proportion between the inflicted punishment and the seriousness of the crime or offence committed.
Regardless of the type of punishment, it can never be considered as a crime; it is always the exercise, by the state, of a strict obligation.
Obviously, to punish does not consist merely in striking or killing in self-defence, as if it were a snake that is crushed or a mad dog that is shot down. The extent of this right must be subject to the requirements of justice and of social usefulness. Such is its purpose. It is in this perspective, it seems to me, that an answer to the problem of capital punishment should be sought.
To punish by death is obviously the ultimate resort of justice, and this punishment should be inflicted only to murderers in full possession of their faculties. On this point, it seems that our Criminal Code does not sufficiently take into account the latest medical data. Feeble-minded and neurotic people should not be condemned to death. I have known some who have been condemned to death and whose sense of responsibility was undoubtedly impaired. In those cases, when I was acting as crown attorney, I made a point of recommending a commutation, and on every occasion, it was granted.
In this respect, it is clear that the Criminal Code should be amended. Under our system of law, through the machinery of procedure,

an accused is free to use every means of defence. Presumed innocence is a sound principle, while, on the other hand, when it comes to establishing the degree of responsibility, it may prove a handicap. Judges and juries are not always acquainted with the context of an offence, the course followed by the accused in committing it, the external influences that prompted him to act and against which he was helpless. Since medicine, especially in psychiatry and psychology, has made great progress in this respect, criminologists and even jurists should resort more and more to those sciences.
Therefore, I wholly agree with the view expressed on this subject in the January 13 last issue of Le Soleil. I quote:
Discussions perhaps indicate that the time has come to widen legal concepts regarding the death penalty; from a practical point of view, we know as a fact that, since Prime Minister Diefenbaker took office, a good many people who were condemned to death have benefited from a commutation of their sentence.
May I add that this was the spirit in which I supported the principle of the Drysdale bill.
But to place all murderers on the same level, to inflict upon them only the penalty that the Criminal Code reserves for infanticide, manslaughter, rape or robbery, would seem to me quite contrary to the standards of justice. That is the fundamental reason why I cannot get myself to support his bill. Justice requires a certain hierarchy in the penalties and that is a principle that the state must respect and enforce.
We are told that it has never been proved that the prospect of hanging truly served to save on life. What a serious mistake. I had the opportunity to talk with prisoners who were jailed for robberies. I remember one man who, to rob a bank, had used a toy revolver to scare the manager and the employees. His reason for not using a genuine one, was precisely the fear of killing and of the fatal results which might have followed. If we abolish capital punishment completely, those useless precautions will no longer be taken by the bandits.
May I add that I know of at least three cases where the murderers, after acquittal in two of those cases, and, in the other, after commutation, were able to commit further crimes and thus take the life of three innocent victims.
Despite all the pity we might feel for the man who is to receive the supreme punish-

ment, reason requires that we avoid endangering the lives that society has the responsibility to protect. And I believe that the hierarchy of judicial and executive powers which always scrupulously examines a death sentence, offers all the guarantees which are humanly possible to obtain. It is very easy for anyone to claim that a judicial error has taken place, when we know about a case only through the prism of a pamphlet or a morbid and noisy propaganda.
When a murder is committed, the population wants to lynch the murderer, but soon, this sentiment of revenge is replaced by a quite different one which sometimes tends to make a god of the criminal. All of us are more or less inclined to those sentimental contradictions. That is why I believe the problem of capital punishment should be resolved on the firm ground of the principles of sound philosophy, otherwise we risk getting confused and arriving at an extremely dangerous solution for the possible victims and for society.
In Berne, Switzerland, in 1912, a congress of jurists was held for the purpose of asking the government to re-establish capital punishment, because of an increase of criminality at the time.
A noted criminologist, professor Kebedgy, made these very appropriate remarks:
We are faced with murderers against whom it is necessary to defend ourselves through the most appropriate means. It has been proved to the hilt that penalties by loss of freedom have no deterrent effect on those criminals; they still have the hope of recovering their freedom one day, if necessary by murdering their guards; in any case, those penalties are too humane compared to the bestiality shown by those hopeless criminals.
Then, expressing the concern of the Swiss people, the learned professor went on to say:
Therefore, all the people of Switzerland are interested in the drawing up of a penal legislation providing an effective safeguard for their life. Too much thought has been given up to now to the criminal, and not enough to the victim and the family of the victim.
Somebody said: "The death penalty is as ignominious for the society which imposes it as for the one on whom it is inflicted". "We have reached," it has been said, "such a degree of civilization that we must rid ourselves of that monstruous vestige of the middle ages". With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I say that I disagree with such a weak argument which ignores what we inherited from the antiquity, the middle ages and the renaissance and in which, all in all, it seems to me there is more wheat than tares.
Furthermore, a century which has known concentration camps, torture practised like
Capital Punishment
a science, mass murders of innocent hostages, crematoria where people are thrown alive, bombing of civilians, execution for crimes of opinion, mock trials under laws which did not exist at the time when those acts which they now consider a crime were committed, that century I feel is no better than past centuries. I am sorry to say that mankind has hardly improved, even if science and technical achievements may now raise our knowledge to the stars that surround our planet.
I hope with all my heart that the day will come when all those evils afflicting this century will disappear. I look forward to the day when the whole Canadian nation will be satisfied by experience that we have no need of an executioner to protect us. That experience has not yet been made, and statistics in such matters will never convince me, as there are so many intangible factors that cut and dried figures may not express. Yet, those intangible factors are the very ones that differentiate people from one another and the only ones that could shed some light on the problems of responsibility and selfdetermination.
Now, I also think that, when it really becomes feasible and if the blessed day of disarmed peace for individuals and nations ever comes, we should welcome final and absolute abolition of capital punishment as a tremendous progress and advance, not so much in human law, but with regard to the conscience of men who will at last have understood the infinite value that must be attached to human life.

Mr. Speaker, as this debate draws to the close of its second day it is inevitable that there should be a certain amount of repetition. If in the next few minutes I offend in that particular regard, I ask your indulgence and the indulgence of my fellow members.
We are discussing a bill which if carried and forwarded to fruition will remove from the lips of supreme court judges across Canada those heartbreaking and tragic words, "You will be hanged by the neck until you are dead". Participation in a debate of this kind is rather difficult for a layman. My good friend from Niagara Falls called himself a layman this afternoon; I do so tonight. I use the term to differentiate between those who are trained in the law, of which we have many in this house-particularly those who are trained in criminal law and have practiced criminal law-and those of us who lack that training. I use it to distinguish between those who have given months and

Capital Punishment
possibly years of study to a subject of this kind, to wit the mover and seconder of the bill, as compared to others of us who have gathered our impression of murder and murderers through newspapers, possibly casually on our way through life.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, perhaps there is some virtue in the expression of a layman, because he may express to a far greater degree than the trained criminal lawyer or the man versed in law the viewpoint of the man on the street. Because of the limited opportunity of the man on the street, he only reads about murders. You know, Mr. Speaker, it is a curious fact that there is a perverse streak in most of us which makes a murder and a murder trial required reading. When a layman attempts to speak on this bill he faces possible criticism. There will always be critics, and some of them may be cruel. If one is against abolition, against the bill, then one is a sadist; if one is for the bill, for the abolition of capital punishment, he may be termed a sentimentalist. The term "sentiment" has been used in this house several times today, and I should like to say that with regard to this particular subject, my impression, is it has become rampant. May I hasten to add that this house has not become sentimental; the sentimentality is outside the house, and I think we can thank our good friends of the press, radio and television for engendering a great deal of it.
Let me say that before leaving home to attend this session I viewed a television show with the title, "Shadow of a Pale Horse". Why that particular exhibition was presented on a Sunday night during the family hour I will never know, but it was the most profound piece of propaganda work against capital punishment I can imagine. Since that time-[DOT] and that seemed to be the genesis of this great outpouring of sentiment-we have had column after column in our daily papers, article after article in our weekly supplements, and magazine articles in great number.
What is the theme of most of this writing? It constantly recurs. The theme has to do with the poor, dear murderer, his last day, his last meal, his last hour, his mounting of the gallows, the callous hangman, the reactions of the official witnesses. As I say, we have had a great outpouring of this type of publicity. All of the factors surrounding the hanging have been fully portrayed. We have been exposed, I am sorry to say, to sentimentality. In fact I might even call it sickening sentimentality.
What have not been portrayed, at least not within my knowledge, have been the last moments of the murdered child, woman or man. What have not been portrayed have

been the agonies and the heartbreaks of the survivors, not for a day, a week or three months, but for years.
It is quite true that the seconder of this bill made a passing reference when speaking on the bill to the survivors of a murdered person, and he said, in effect: Don't let us make a widow and fatherless children when we hang a murderer just because the murdered person left a widow and fatherless children. Mr. Speaker, to me that is hardly appropriate. No one remembers the bereaved after a short time. I can remember attending two or three funerals of persons murdered. They were gigantic affairs. Everyone attended. The flowers were magnificent. But I can also remember that a few months later the widow was applying for widow's allowance and wondering how she was going to feed her brood.
This afternoon the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) traced briefly the safeguards which are thrown around a person who is tried for murder. It seems to me we might dwell on that subject again for a few moments. Let me repeat I am not a lawyer, but I have a tremendous admiration and respect for the Canadian judicial system. It is patterned after that of Great Britain and it is respected throughout the entire world.
A murder is committed. A suspect is arraigned and, as the hon. member for Stormont said, the first step is a preliminary hearing before a magistrate. That may be a technicality. If there is sufficient evidence to justify sending the accused to a higher court, he goes. Very seldom is he dismissed by a magistrate. He goes before a jury and a trial judge and, as my hon. friend said, the trial judge is eminently fair and completely impartial. Those of us who have lived in Canada -and I am speaking particularly, now, of my own part of the country-have grown up with some of our judges. I can think of seven or eight justices in the province of Alberta whom I know intimately and whom I have known for many years. They are men of very high calibre, and certainly a murderer who appears before a trial judge in a supreme court in any province of Canada is assured of an impartial umpire.
Should the accused person be convicted, his case then goes to the court of appeal. Here you have the collective wisdom of several judges. The bench is composed of men of wisdom and high quality; men without any interest in that particular case except to see that justice is done; men with a tremendous knowledge of the law and a deep understanding of humanity. The next step is, of course, the supreme court, another outstanding court Lastly we come to the cabinet. Cabinets come and go, but certainly a cabinet in a country

such as Canada attracts to its membership the highest type of mentality available, the type of person who is activated entirely by a desire to be fair in the consideration of matters of this kind, and to see that justice prevails.
It is all very well to say, as some have said, that a poor man has no recourse to these various tribunals. I can think of no poor murderer that I ever knew or heard of who was denied access to this procedure. Indeed I can remember public subscriptions being made to make sure that such people received the full consideration of all these tribunals, and I find it hard to understand the statement made by some of my colleagues that if you are poor you hang but if you are rich you escape.
A further word with respect to the careful analysis of crimes of murder which is given by these various bodies. I well remember- and the speech of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) reminded me of this-a very famous case defended by the hon. member's late father, a beloved member of this house for many years, the late A. L. Smith. This crime was of particular interest to me because the boy accused of it lived in the house next door and he was tried for murder, found guilty, and sentenced to be hung. A retrial was ordered. The young man went through the second trial and eventually was acquitted. There was a scintilla of doubt, and I feel, as a layman, that where there is a scintilla of doubt the accused is favoured.
We have heard a great many statistics, and a lot of work has been done documenting the case for and against capital punishment. We have had statistics from Luxembourg, New Zealand, Sweden and some of the middle western states. We have been told that the abolition of capital punishment has reduced the incidence of murder. We have also been told that the maintenance of capital punishment has increased the number of murders. I have been wondering since this phase of the discussion first came to the front what is the reason for the favourable statistics from such places as Luxembourg, Sweden and the mid-western states, and it occurred to me that part of the answer lies in the fact that these countries have homogeneous populations. They are all one people. We in Canada -and this is one of our great glories-are not a homogeneous people; we are a heterogeneous people. We have in Canada a mixture of all the bloods of Europe and some from outside, and we have the volatile temperament which goes with certain races and it will be some years before we become homogeneous. Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate I should like to say that I hope the debate will prove exhaustive and that it will bring some positive results. The subject with which we are dealing today has come to the fore in recent years. On June 27, 1956 a parliamentary committee appointed to look into this matter submitted its report on this question and it recommended three things; first, retention of the death penalty; second, substitution of electrocution or a gas chamber for hanging; and, third, the abolition of executions for convicted murderers 18 years or under. With these recommendations I do not quarrel. In my opinion they are just as sound today as when they were made.
However, I should like to elaborate on the committee's second recommendation that electrocution or a gas chamber be substituted for hanging. Death by hanging is a brutal thing. The anxiety of some persons awaiting sentence of death over the possibility of inefficiency on the part of the hangman is something to be considered. Of the 42 states of the United States of America retaining the death penalty only 9 retain hanging. Twenty four have adopted electrocution, 8 have chosen lethal gas and one,

Utah, gives a choice of shooting or hanging. Only 9, as I said before, have retained hanging.
There is also in my opinion the desirability of having some centrally designated place set aside for the purpose of execution. This I think, would also provide that efficiency to which I have already referred. I am one of those who believe that there is no harm whatsoever in keeping the death penalty on the statute books even if we may not ever have to use it. Those who have spoken in favour of abolition have not dealt with the case of the convicted murderer imprisoned for life who murders his guard and perhaps murders again. What can society do under circumstances where capital punishment does not exist? I am afraid there is no answer to this question if capital punishment should be abolished.
I believe capital punishment is a deterrent, notwithstanding the statistics, because the number of people who have been deterred can never be known or even guessed at. I agree wholeheartedly with the remarks made by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue (Mr. Martineau) this afternoon with regard to the question of a deterrent.
I believe, the greatest deterrent of all is that basic instinct of man, self-preservation. I believe that when any murderer decides to follow that path with premeditation he must take this into consideration otherwise, in my opinion as a physician, he would not be a sane man. We have heard much regarding statistics which supposedly prove that capital punishment is not a deterrent. I am not in agreement with that view, however. I should like to put on the record part of an editorial which is to be found in the February 1, 1960 edition of Christianity Today which is published in Washington, D.C., with regard to the question of statistics in the "modern debate on the death penalty". I quote:
Statistics have been cited both to support and to oppose the claim that execution deters capital crimes. But a Christian lawyer, Eoscoe G. Sap-penfield of Geneva, Illinois, reminds us of an observation made by Judge Marcus Kavanaugh of Cook county superior court, Illinois, before the Detroit college of law.
May I remind you, sir, that Michigan does not impose the death penalty.
"Detroit with 1,600,000 residents, has had 484 homicides in two years, while Windsor, only 20 minutes from here, and with 75,000 residents, has had no homicides. Do you need any further arguments for capital punishment?" When capital crime statistics are unfavourable in jurisdictions

that impose the death penalty, Attorney Sappen-field adds, the law is not a deterrent because it is not really enforced."
I should like to commend the present government for their record in commuting 32 out of 40 sentences reviewed during the past 2J years. Here I see the greatest degree of consideration being extended to convicted murderers, despite the fact that under British law I believe there has never been a conviction made in a case in which there has been reasonable doubt in the minds of the jury. I believe also that our rules relative to the admission of evidence are very strict, and are designed to protect the accused. Some of those who have spoken here, especially the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) whose experience in this field goes back for many years, have presented this question in what 1 would consider to be a very sound way. Capital Punishment
they all tend to support the principle which I believe is important, that is that capital punishment be retained on the statute books of our country, even though it may never be used in the years which lie ahead.
There is an important issue which has to be faced by every member in this house in giving consideration to the bill which is before us, and that is the moral issue. As a physician I have to make decisions every day in my life having in mind the moral laws, having in mind the moral question. In so far as this particular bill is concerned, I think the No. 1 consideration is the moral issue. Some of those who support this bill claim that they do so on moral grounds, that it is wrong even for society to take a life. However, the bill permits society to take a life in the case of treason. How my hon. friends resolve this dilemma, I do not know. I do believe the moral issue should be considered fully. These are my beliefs in this field.
I believe a policeman, acting on behalf of society, who is confronted with a situation which results in the killing of a lawbreaker is morally justified. I believe that an individual, criminally attacked and acting in self-defence who kills is morally justified. I further believe, that the state has the right to use capital punishment in cases which the state considers to be serious crimes. In that category today in our country we place treason and murder. There can be, from time to time, other serious crimes of such a nature that they would warrant, in my opinion, capital punishment if society is to defend itself and if it is to preserve itself.
Many leading churchmen have expressed the view that capital punishment should not be abolished. The Archbishop of Canterbury in the Church of England believes that this is strictly a matter which should be dealt with on the grounds of whether it is in the interests of public safety, peace, order and good government. On that basis he believes that the death penalty should be retained. I certainly agree with him. Another leading churchman, Rev. E. L. H. Taylor, in his role as chaplain to the Canadian Legion, stated in an article published in the Toronto Star of February 16, 1960:
The Christian church, far from being traditionally opposed to capital punishment, was responsible for its original introduction into the legal systems of western Europe.
As I said before, in our country, where there are mitigating circumstances such as a jury's recommendation for mercy, that is

given very serious consideration. The whole matter is then considered by the department of the Solicitor General, through his experts. Then there is consideration given by the deputy minister of justice, the Minister of Justice and then the entire cabinet. A final decision is made and the governor in council is advised as to whether or not there shall be commutation. In fact, therefore, there are all kinds of safeguards to protect an innocent man from capital punishment. I really believe we have a most effective system and I doubt that under our system any really innocent person could possibly be executed.
Mention has been made during this debate of the fact that in New Zealand capital punishment had been abolished but was reinstituted at a future date. From time to time in the life of a parliamentarian, Mr. Speaker, he is faced with a measure that creates difficulties for him in reaching a decision.
