But I also want to pay my compliments to many other speakers in this debate. As many other hon. members have said, I think this has been a wide-open, conscientious debate where hon. members have spoken according to their conscience or belief.
I would like to pay special tribute to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney). I think that anybody who came in here and did not understand the issue before him should be convinced by his argument. It would be very difficult, with a man with the experience of defending criminals which this hon. gentleman has had, not to be convinced, I will grant him that. However, I would like to say that in my experience lawyers associated with a certain type of case become very much sympathetic toward that type of case, and his argument had no effect on me.
I should like to read this particular section which the bill suggests should replace the existing section 206 of the act:
Every one who commits murder is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be sentenced to imprisonment for life.
Those last words mean nothing. There is only one way you can vote on this question today, unless you want the criminals who commit the worst crimes in this country to be running abroad. I feel very strongly on this issue. I am one of just a few hon. members of this house who sat on the special committee. We heard the evidence. We saw

Capital Punishment
the witnesses. We listened to their stories, and the majority of our committee came to a very sound conclusion, in my personal opinion, and we recommended that capital punishment be retained. We also recommended, of course, that it might be reviewed.
Capital punishment has been narrowed down to two crimes, and the one we are discussing in particular is murder, the worst of all crimes. I defy anyone to prove to me that a man who commits murder ever gives any consideration to the person he murders. As far as I am concerned I am not prepared to give any consideration to the murderer.
That does not mean to say that I am in full accord with the type of execution, and on this point I think there is a great deal of confusion. I know there is a lot of confusion in the minds of the public. I know that they are mixing the two questions, one of conviction and the other of execution. They should be considered separately, but in the minds of the public they are not considered separately; and I know from listening to the speeches of hon. members in this house that they are somewhat confused. I will admit that it is rather difficult for those who have not much experience in criminal matters to think about these two things separately.
The next thing is that I am not interested in the deterrent. Statistics? We had books of them. We had briefs full of them. You can get statistics to prove the case either way, depending on which way you are thinking. Statistics have been quoted here, but they mean nothing. What have we got a law for in this country anyway? Did we not start back in the beginning to draw up a law for the protection of society for order and good government? If we are going to maintain it we must maintain punishment also to keep it worth while. I suppose I am the only speaker who has mentioned that word. Everyone has refrained from using the word "punishment". If you break the gaming laws you are punished by a fine. If you break the liquor laws you may be punished with a jail sentence and a fine. Every law we have must carry a punishment if it is broken, and there is no reason why the worst crime of all should not carry the heaviest penalty of all, the death sentence.
Let me say that I respect the opinions of these good-thinking people who go about the country trying to be reformists. I think most of them are sincere but I do not agree with their arguments. I will agree with the hon. member for Parkdale, who was so fair. He said that it is not the only deterrent, and I agree. He made another statement with which I also agree. He said, if I understood

him aright, that it was not morally wrong. A lot of hon. members in this house and also people outside argue that it is morally wrong to put a man to death after he has committed murder and was proven to have done so. I think, if I quote the hon. member for Parkdale correctly, he said we are morally entitled to do it but we are not morally obligated to do it. I agree with that; I think it is a very fair statement.
Another argument which was raised was that of error. In my experience, and I think it can be proved by the debates in this house, we represent here a cross section of this country and amongst us are professional men, businessmen, farmers, representatives of many forms of work and labour. We represent in the best sense of the word the type of men who sit on a jury. You get a crosssection of the community, all good, law abiding, honest reliable men and women, and in all my experience I will tell you right now, and any other lawyer will back me up, in nine cases out of ten the jury is usually right.
I have not got time to tell stories to illustrate these things or to go into the history, but if the jury are hearing the evidence on a person who has been sent to trial they are very careful and, as they are warned by the court, if there is any kind of doubt they will give the benefit of that doubt to the accused person. The prisoner has every chance in the world to get off scot-free, because the old theory is that it is better that 99 men should go free than that one innocent person should be condemned. Under our system here in Canada there has been no evidence in a criminal case-the crime of all crimes-that an innocent man has been convicted. I will go further and say that when a man or a woman is convicted and all the subsequent legal steps open to them have been taken, including appeals on legal questions and so on, the matter then goes before a remission board. I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden) said that all these cases were considered very carefully. Certainly, within the last few years, they have been.
I remember well that when the committee was sitting the then minister of justice of this country, Mr. Stuart Garson, told us that every aspect of these cases was reviewed; the mental state of the convicted person, whether his offence was a crime of passion, or due to drunkenness, and so on. Submissions are made by a lawyer on behalf of the accused, the judge who tried the case files a long report, relatives of the accused may submit briefs and, in short, the man is given every chance in the world. There is a medical examination. When all these things have been

taken into consideration, if any of these factors can be interpreted in favour of the accused man, he is not executed.
For this reason I was surprised to hear hon. members here today, and on the last day when this debate took place, saying we should abolish capital punishment because the government was using the royal prerogative too often. At least the opinion seemed to be getting around: what is the use of sentencing these people; the government is going to let them off, so why not change the law making it possible for the judge to sentence them to life imprisonment. Life imprisonment does not mean a thing under our law. Until that is fixed there is no way in which anyone can vote with regard to this bill unless he is an abolitionist and wants murderers to be running around this country after a very short period in the penitentiary. In my opinion, members of this house are bound to vote to retain capital punishment until there are a lot of other changes made.
One hon. member said it was unfortunate that a person convicted of murder had to go through weeks of torment before his execution or before he found out that he would be reprieved and sent to prison. I may be awfully hard boiled, I do not know, but I will tell you there are a lot of things I can be sentimental about just as much as the other fellow, but unfortunately I cannot be sentimental about the man who strikes down a little child or a woman and does not care what sort of crime he commits. I consider such crimes to be premeditated crimes, and nothing is too bad for that man. I think he should be executed, to put it shortly, and I think in fact that this is the type of criminal who is subjected to the death penalty under our present system. This is the only type of criminal who is being executed. Everything is taken into consideration. It is only when a man was not drunk at the time he committed his crime; when he did it in a fit of passion; when he did it deliberately and knowingly, that the full penalty is exacted.
I may say, incidentally that I have not too much sympathy with a man who commits murder in a fit of passion, either. But if a man goes out armed with a gun or other instrument with intention to commit a burglary, and makes up his mind that he is going to kill anyone who gets in his way, I consider that to be premeditated murder and I have no sympathy with it. As to the other type of murderer, the man or woman who is upset psychologically, I do not think hon. members will find that any of them are executed.
I feel very strongly on this subject, and many of the things which I think of saying
Capital Punishment
have been said before. However, before I finish I should like to say to those hon. members who are not able to make up their minds that they are either badly confused, just as many people outside this house are, because they do not understand the procedure during the trial of a criminal, or else there is some other reason why they do not want to make up their minds. It seems to me that any man who has been sent here as a member of parliament should be capable of making up his mind one way or the other. It is our business to give leadership to our constituencies. It is not for us to follow them. For example, how many people in my constituency know what steps are taken from the time a person is apprehended until the day of his reprieve or execution? A very small percentage, I would say. I have talked to people in Ottawa and I find that they do not understand our procedure. Besides, there is another thing: they are mixing the execution with the conviction.
I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that most of the people of this country who are sound, solid citizens, feel that the law of this country should be observed. In order to make this country safe for society we cannot allow these people who deliberately plan to kill and do kill to suffer, in the end, less than an execution. They should be removed from society. As long as they are imprisoned they will not be permanently removed from society. As an hon. member said a moment ago, they could commit as many murders as they like and there would be nothing we could do about it but put them in prison.
I could not support this bill and have no hesitation in taking a strong stand against it. However, I appreciate and respect the opinions that have been expressed by the mover of the bill and those hon. members who have spoken in favour of it. I cannot help but wonder, though, if some of them really understand the nature of this question. I wonder if some have had terrible crimes committed in their constituencies, practically on -their door steps. I wonder if they have, as it were, come face to face with heinous crimes.
After a man is apprehended and convicted several months elapse before the time for his execution arrives. People have forgotten the revulsion they felt at first hearing of the crime. The newspapers and television and many good people in the community sort of play up the terrible fact of hanging. I do not care whether you do it by hanging, electrocution or the gas chamber-I am not particularly stuck on any of these means of execution-but I feel that murderers should pay the supreme penalty. I say you pay your money and you take your choice.

Capital Punishment
We want to make Canada a safe, happy society. We want this to he a place where we can feel that our wives and daughters will be safe on the streets even in the evenings. We want it to be a place where you will feel safe walking down the street with a thousand dollars in your pocket, although I do not imagine that many hon. members will ever have that experience. I feel that the death penalty serves as a deterrent and keeps our country safe.
We must remember that our country is different from England and various European countries. This all came out in the joint committee where this question was considered. It was pointed out that Canadians lives alongside another country that has a different outlook on life and plenty of crime. We do not want to make our backyard a resting place or haven for people from across the line who are evading the law. One way we can rid society of these people is to have United States criminals come over here and commit these serious crimes, and we will take them out of society.
I am pleased to have had the opportunity of presenting my views on this bill and I am sorry that I must inform the mover of the bill that I am going to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, in this debate in the house there has been a great deal of discussion of the problems concerning capital punishment. For me the problem can be resolved by answering the following six questions.
The first question is, is the death penalty an effective deterrent? Second, is the imposition of the death penalty un-Christian? Third, are innocent persons ever hanged? Of course, bound up in this question is the question of whether or not insane persons are ever hanged. The fourth question is, is life imprisonment a sufficiently effective protection for the public in cases of crimes warranting a sentence of capital punishment? Fifth, does the carrying out of the death sentence brutalize those who are involved in its execution and does it lower the moral tone in the community in which it was carried out? Sixth, is capital punishment merely retributive justice?
Before dealing with the deterrents I should like to take issue with the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) who suggested that the burden of proof as to whether this bill should be supported is on those of us who do not support the bill. I would suggest that the burden of proof as to whether the law should be changed is on those who support it. It is their duty to make out a sufficiently strong case as to convince us that the law should be changed.

Many statistics are available in relation to the question of deterrents. Statistics in relation to this question do not impress me in the least because in the first place we have no means of knowing how many people were deterred from committing the crime of murder and, in the second place, the crime rate and the kind of crime in any country depends on various external factors which make it impossible to determine it statistically. The moral climate of a country determines the crime rate and thus the murder rate. The economic conditions of a country also have a bearing on the matter. One would have to rationalize these problems before one could say statistically that the murder rate has been increased or decreased by the abolition of the death sentence.
For guidance in this question I feel that we must look elsewhere to those who have had great experience in the administration of justice, in police work, prison management, the rehabilitation of criminals, judges, criminal lawyers, police experts, prison wardens, penologists and others. Here, too, opinion is divided, but I feel that the opinions of those in whom I place the greatest reliance is that the death penalty is an effective deterrent in many kinds of killings and for that reason if for no other I would oppose this bill.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) who has so eloquently stated the case for opposition to this bill was a member in 1955 and 1956 of the joint committee of this house and the other place which made a long and exhaustive study of the statistics involved in crimes and also conducted an examination of witnesses and experts in these matters. The conclusions embodied in the report of that committee state in part:
The committee has concluded that the death penalty is most likely to operate as a restraint and a deterrent to professional criminals who are obviously not deterred from crime by the risk of imprisonment alone, and that it is necessary to retain capital punishment to minimize the tendency of Canadian criminals to use violence in the commission of other crimes.
Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
